top10_weekly.title: Glymphatic Dysfunction Drives High-Urea-Induced Neurodegeneration in Parkinson's Disease.
top10_weekly.abstract: BACKGROUND: Disruption of brain urea homeostasis has been implicated in neurodegenerative disorders, yet its molecular mechanisms remain elusive. This study aimed to investigate how urea metabolic disturbance drives neurodegeneration through astrocytic polarity impairment and to identify potential therapeutic targets. METHODS: A high-urea mouse model was generated by urea transporter B (UT-B) knockout. Pharmacological inhibition and genetic intervention were applied to examine dipeptidyl peptidase-like protein 6 (DPP6), protein kinase C eta (PKCη), and aquaporin-4 (AQP4) expression and localization in astrocytes. Glymphatic clearance, α-synuclein (α-syn) pathology propagation, and dopaminergic neurodegeneration were evaluated. RESULTS: Urea upregulated astrocytic DPP6, activated PKCη signaling, and induced AQP4 endocytosis with loss of membrane polarity, leading to impaired glymphatic clearance, accelerated α-syn spread, and dopaminergic neuronal degeneration. Mechanistically, the DPP6-PKCη axis directly regulated AQP4 membrane localization; inhibiting this pathway pharmacologically or genetically rescued all pathological phenotypes. CONCLUSIONS: This study reveals that urea metabolic disruption promotes neurodegenerative progression via the DPP6-PKCη-AQP4 pathway by compromising astrocytic polarity, offering new therapeutic targets for Parkinson's disease. © 2026 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.

top10_weekly.title: BHLHE22 monoallelic and biallelic variants cause a neurodevelopmental disorder with agenesis of the corpus callosum, intellectual disability, abnormal muscle tone and movement abnormalities.
top10_weekly.abstract: BACKGROUND: BHLHE22 encodes a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor (bHLH) expressed exclusively in the retina and central nervous system (CNS), and functions as an important regulator of neuronal differentiation. However, BHLHE22 has not yet been associated with a Mendelian neurodevelopmental or neurological disorder. METHODS: Fifteen individuals from thirteen unrelated families carrying BHLHE22 variants identified by exome sequencing were collected through an international collaboration. RESULTS: De novo missense variants located in the highly conserved helix-loop-helix domain of the protein were found in six individuals, and one recurrent homozygous frameshift variant, NP_689627.1:p.Gly74AlafsTer18, was found in nine individuals. Frequent clinical features include absent or limited speech (10/13), delayed or impaired motor abilities (11/13), intellectual disability (9/12), partial or complete agenesis of the corpus callosum (12/15), involuntary movements and/or stereotypies (11/13), and abnormal muscle tone (13/13), depending on data availability. Two individuals developed spastic paraplegia, without intellectual disability (ID) or callosal anomalies. One individual had moderate developmental delay and ID, but without callosal anomalies. CONCLUSION: Collectively, our data establish BHLHE22 as a previously unrecognized neurodevelopmental disease gene. Disruption of BHLHE22, through either dominant or recessive variants, results in a distinct syndrome characterized by abnormalities in brain development, cognition, tone, and movement.

top10_weekly.title: Gαi2 promotes microtubule-driven incorporation of neurofilaments to stabilise nascent axons in vivo.
top10_weekly.abstract: Axon initiation is a critical step in the establishment of neuronal morphology. However, the mechanisms regulating stable axon initiation during embryonic development remain poorly understood. Here, using fixed-tissue super-resolution and high-resolution live-tissue imaging in the developing chick spinal cord, we reveal that stable axon initiation is characterised by microtubule-directed neurofilament accumulation in the emerging axon, and identify the multifunctional G-protein Gαi2 as a regulator of this process. Before axon initiation, microtubule network orientation shifts towards the site of the future axon where coiled Gαi2-associated neurofilaments accumulate asymmetrically before unfurling into the initiating axon behind microtubules. Crucially, Gαi2 is associated with neurofilaments and microtubules at their points of contact. Gαi2 depletion reduces engagement between these cytoskeletal networks and leads to impaired passage of neurofilaments into initiating axons and disrupted axon outgrowth, supporting a role for Gαi2 in regulating microtubule-driven incorporation of neurofilaments in nascent axons. These findings advance mechanistic understanding of polarity establishment and provide insight into cytoskeletal regulation during axon formation.

top10_weekly.title: Microglial NUS1 deficiency drives dopaminergic neurodegeneration through intercellular iron dysregulation in Parkinson's disease models.
top10_weekly.abstract: The selective loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta is a defining feature of Parkinson's disease (PD), yet its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. NUS1, which encodes neurite outgrowth inhibitor-B receptor (NgBR), was recently identified as a PD risk gene. Here we show that NgBR is highly expressed in microglia, where its deficiency drives progressive PD-like motor deficits and dopaminergic neurodegeneration via the LCN2-SLC22A17 iron-transport axis in mice. NgBR deficiency in mouse and human microglia triggers endoplasmic reticulum stress and PERK-ATF4-NUPR1 signaling, which preferentially induces LCN2-mediated iron efflux over cytokine release. Subsequently, microglia-derived iron-loaded Holo-LCN2, but not iron-free Apo-LCN2, is internalized by SLC22A17, a receptor highly expressed in dopaminergic neurons, leading to iron overload and ferroptosis. Pharmacological inhibition of LCN2-SLC22A17 axis or ferroptosis alleviated dopaminergic neuron loss and PD-like symptoms caused by microglial NgBR deficiency in vitro and in vivo. Our findings identify disrupted intercellular iron homeostasis as a pathological driver of PD and highlight the LCN2-SLC22A17 axis as a potential therapeutic target.

top10_weekly.title: The N-Ank protein Ankrd24 shapes neurons and couples to syndapin and the F-actin promoter Cobl-like.
top10_weekly.abstract: Proper neuromorphogenesis is pivotal for neuronal network formation and brain function. The underlying cell biological tasks are complex, as they include both remodeling of membrane topologies and of cytoskeletal structures. Yet, mechanisms coordinating these two different cell biological functions are largely unknown. Here, we molecularly and functionally characterize ankyrin repeat domain-containing protein 24 (Ankrd24) and demonstrate that this ankyrin-repeat protein is able to interact with and bend membranes and mechanistically and functionally belongs to the recently proposed N-Ank superfamily. Mutational analyses revealed that the N-Ank functions of Ankrd24 are indispensable for Ankrd24's role in neuromorphogenesis. Ankrd24 furthermore physically cooperated with the F-BAR domain protein syndapin I (PACSIN1) and with Cobl-like (Cobll1), a protein promoting actin filament formation, by ternary complex formation. Both partners were critical for Ankrd24-mediated dendritic arborization. This identified Ankrd24 as critical part of a larger, coordinated effort in inducing new dendritic branches. Our work thereby sheds light on the molecular mechanisms underlying the complex task of proper neuronal arbor development.

top10_weekly.title: Opposing Patterns of the Histone Variant MacroH2A1.1 in Fmr1 Knockout and BTBR T+ Itpr3tf/J Mouse Models of Autism Spectrum Disorder.
top10_weekly.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) exhibits substantial heterogeneity, wherein genetic and idiopathic forms may converge on shared core phenotypes through divergent molecular pathways. The histone variant macroH2A1.1, implicated in chromatin repression and DNA repair, has been linked to behavioral alterations opposite to core ASD features when depleted systemically. However, its regional and cell-type-specific regulation in genetic versus idiopathic ASD models remains unclear. We investigated macroH2A1.1 expression across the dorsal striatum, hippocampus, and medial prefrontal cortex in Fmr1 knockout (Fragile X syndrome model) and BTBR T+ Itpr3tf/J (idiopathic ASD model) mice. Quantitative PCR and imaging analyses revealed opposing patterns: BTBR mice showed region-specific mRNA downregulation and increased strongly stained macroH2A1.1-positive nuclei, whereas Fmr1 knockout mice exhibited reduced strong staining with increased weak staining, specific to neurons and not astrocytes, independent of significant mRNA changes. Bulk RNA-seq meta-analysis and pseudobulk single-cell transcriptomics further identified pathway-level enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation, chromatin remodeling, and transcriptional repression functional gene sets in unmatched public datasets (BTBR striatum; FXS hippocampus and cortex), with pronounced neuron-astrocyte divergence in Fmr1 knockout cortex. These findings underscore distinct epigenetic regulatory mechanisms in genetic and idiopathic ASD models.

top10_weekly.title: An integrated human forebrain organoid reveals microglia-mediated CD8+ T cell recruitment and neuroimmune dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease pathology.
top10_weekly.abstract: Genetic evidence implicates immune dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the neuroimmune mechanisms operating in human tissue remain poorly defined. Here, we establish a modular human forebrain organoid platform that systematically integrates human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia and CD8+ T cells to reconstitute multicellular AD pathology. This system enables functional interrogation of both innate and adaptive immune components in a human-relevant context. Using this platform, we demonstrate that microglia mediate amyloid-β clearance and neuronal maturation but also drive inflammatory activation and recruit CD8+ T cells through CCL4/5 signaling via CCR1/5 and CXCR3, establishing a neuroinflammatory feedback loop. Pharmacological targeting of CCR5 or CXCR3 blocks T cell recruitment and modulates autophagy in a microglia-dependent manner. This modular organoid platform provides a versatile tool for dissecting neuron-immune interactions and enables cell-type-specific therapeutic screening in human neuroinflammatory disease models.

top10_weekly.title: 53BP1 as a cofactor in the activation of the p53-family transcriptional program: A correlative multimodal microscopy approach.
top10_weekly.abstract: Understanding how molecular mechanisms regulate cell function in tissues requires approaches that link phenotypes to mechanisms across different spatial scales. Here, we present automated multimodal multiplexed microscopy for image cytometry (A.M3.I.CO), a correlative imaging platform that combines multiscale resolution, from millimeters to nanometers, with automated workflows for high-throughput phenotypic profiling and targeted single-molecule analysis in situ. Applying A.M3.I.CO, we observed that 53BP1 is recruited at transcribed p53 target genes independently of the activating stimulus, providing evidence for the formation of a putative complex between 53BP1, p53, and the basal transcription machinery in single cells, as also supported by in vivo observations in tumor models. Extending our measurements to p63 and p73, we found that 53BP1 localized at p63- and p73-targeted transcription sites, suggesting a broader role in participating in p53 family-dependent transcription. These findings indicate an additional genome-surveillance pathway in transcriptional control regulating diverse cellular functions while establishing A.M3.I.CO as a platform for spatially resolved functional analysis.

top10_weekly.title: Protocol for imaging and analyzing the synaptic coverage of astrocytes with super-resolution STED microscopy in mouse brain slices.
top10_weekly.abstract: Super-resolution has allowed us to image areas previously inaccessible due to the limits of standard microscopy techniques. Here, we present a protocol to determine the astroglial coverage of synapses. We detail the steps to obtain and label mouse brain slices followed by imaging using 3D stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy and analysis using a custom-made Fiji plug-in, with imaging at a lateral resolution of 80 nm. This technique ascertains the interaction between astrocytes and the glial cell's role in signaling and brain region function.

top10_weekly.title: Cas9 nickase-mediated contraction of CAG/CTG repeats is associated with phenotypic improvements in a Huntington's disease mouse model.
top10_weekly.abstract: Expanded CAG/CTG repeats cause more than 15 different diseases that all remain without a disease-modifying treatment. Because repeat length accounts for most of the variation in disease severity, contracting CAG/CTG repeats presents an attractive therapeutic avenue. Here, we show that the CRISPR-Cas9 nickase targeted to CAG/CTG repeats leads to efficient repeat contractions in Huntington's disease (HD) patient-derived neurons and astrocytes and in myotonic dystrophy type 1 patient-derived neurons. The approach was allele selective and free of detectable off-target mutations. Injection of the Cas9 nickase into the striatum of the R6/1 mouse model of HD using adeno-associated viral vectors led to repeat contractions in more than half of striatal neurons. Upon injection, we observed a reduction in the number of inclusion bodies, an improved gene expression profile, and amelioration of locomotion deficits in the open field test. The effects were greater than expected from the contractions induced, suggesting that non-cell autonomous mechanisms may be involved. Our results provide the proof of concept that correction of CAG/CTG repeats can improve HD phenotypes in a mouse disease model.

primary.title: Insights into how JIP3 and JIP4 adaptor proteins relieve the auto-inhibited form of the kinesin-1 motor.
primary.abstract: While our understanding of kinesin autoinhibition mechanisms is advancing, key insights into kinesin activation, especially autoinhibition relieved by cargo-motor adaptors, remain unclear. JIP3 and JIP4 are adaptors that activate kinesin-1 and dynein-dynactin motors, enabling bidirectional transport along microtubules. Here, we characterized the interaction between the kinesin-1 heavy chain, KIF5B, and both JIP3 and JIP4 (JIP3/4), using mutagenesis and binding experiments associated with modelling. We identified the minimal regions of JIP3/4 and KIF5B required for interaction. JIP3/4 binds to the CC4 coiled-coil domain of KIF5B, with no significant interaction detected with the distal tail. Conversely, KIF5B-CC4 binds to the RH1 domain of JIP3/4, with the preceding disordered N-terminus modulating the force of the binding. Notably, JIP3 and JIP4 exhibit ∼40-fold differences in affinity for KIF5B. We performed extensive site-directed mutagenesis on KIF5B-binding regions of JIP3/JIP4 targeting accessible charged residues and sequence differences between JIP3 and JIP4. This revealed multiple weak-affinity binding sites that collectively define an extensive KIF5B-binding surface on the RH1 domain of JIP3. Importantly, the KIF5B-binding surface on JIP3 differs from that of the DLIC (dynein light intermediate chain), confirming no competition between the two motors. Altogether, the fragment and mutant mapping of KIF5B binding to JIP3 and JIP4 presented here provides insights into how the auto-inhibited form of kinesin-1 might be relieved, with the CC4 region playing a central role.

primary.title: Ultrastructural studies reveal a new role for JIP3/MAPK8IP3 in endo-lysosomal maturation within the neuronal cell body.
primary.abstract: In recent years, substantial heterogeneity in lysosomes, in terms of their composition, function, and positioning, has come to be recognized. Despite this, there are gaps in knowledge of our understanding of the molecular basis of lysosome heterogeneity, especially in neurons. To this end, we used electron microscopy to define endolysosomal organelles of human iPSC-derived neurons at the ultrastructural level. Through this, we identify endolysosomal maturation defects within neuronal cell bodies of iNeurons lacking JNK-Interacting Protein 3 (JIP3), a lysosome adaptor previously known to primarily regulate axonal lysosome movement. Loss of JIP3 results in an expansion of immature lysosomes within neuronal soma, along with a concomitant decrease in mature lysosomes. JIP3 loss also leads to delayed trafficking of endocytic cargo through these compartments, implicating JIP3 in the regulation of endolysosomal maturation within neuronal cell bodies. Our studies highlight the utility of electron microscopy in understanding neuronal lysosomal heterogeneity. Additionally, given recent links between JIP3 and a neurodevelopmental disorder, our findings here could provide new insight into mechanisms underlying neurodevelopmental pathology.

primary.title: JIP4 and RILPL1 utilize opposing motor force to dynamically regulate lysosomal tubulation.
primary.abstract: Lysosomes are dynamic organelles that remodel their membrane in response to stimuli. We previously uncovered a process we term LYsosomal Tubulation/sorting driven by LRRK2 (LYTL), wherein damaged lysosomes generate tubules sorted into vesicles. LYTL is orchestrated by the Parkinson's disease kinase LRRK2 that recruits the motor adaptor protein and RHD family member JIP4 to lysosomes. JIP4 enhances LYTL tubule extension toward the plus-end of microtubules. To identify new players involved in LYTL, we mapped the lysosomal proteome after LRRK2 kinase inhibition. We found that RILPL1 is recruited to dysfunctional lysosomes in an LRRK2 kinase activity-dependent manner, facilitated by pRAB proteins. Unlike JIP4, RILPL1 induces retraction of LYTL tubules by binding to p150Glued, thereby moving lysosomal tubules toward the minus-end of microtubules. Our findings emphasize the dynamic regulation of LYTL tubules by two distinct RHD proteins and pRAB effectors, acting as opposing motor adaptor proteins. These opposing forces create a metastable lysosomal membrane deformation, enabling dynamic tubulation events.

primary.title: Disruption of dynactin complex function in intellectual disability.
primary.abstract: Intellectual disability (ID) is a highly prevalent condition affecting approximately 200 millions of people worldwide, characterized by impaired cognitive function. Dynactin complex consists of multiple protein subunits and is required for intracellular trafficking and synaptic homeostasis in developing and mature neurons. Here, we identify deleterious variants of dynactin subunit 4 (DCTN4) in ID pedigrees. DCTN4 ablation in mice results in altered neuronal positioning and apoptosis in neural progenitor cells. Notably, mice carrying the ID-linked DCTN4 variant exhibit cognitive deficits with impaired dendritic development. Cortical neurons with DCTN4 deficiency or variant show reduced levels of various dynactin subunits, suggesting that deficits in dynactin complex affects synaptic function. Furthermore, disruption of the DCTN4-JIP3 complex impairs lysosomal transport and dendritic development as well as synaptic development. Importantly, we showed that damaging variants in another dynactin subunit DCTN2 also disrupt neuronal positioning, reinforcing the critical role of dynactin complex in neurodevelopment and ID pathogenesis. These findings illustrate dysfunctional dynactin complex as a previously unrecognized disease mechanism of ID.

secondary.title: Characterization of a novel inherited splice-site variant in MAPK8IP3 expands the genetic and phenotypic spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: The MAPK8IP3 gene encodes JIP3, a kinesin-1 adapter protein crucial for axonal transport and JNK signaling pathway regulation. This gene exhibits extreme intolerance to loss-of-function variants. Heterozygous pathogenic MAPK8IP3 variants are linked to a neurodevelopmental disorder with or without variable brain abnormalities (NEDBA). This study characterizes a novel inherited canonical splice-site variant identified in a three-generation family. METHODS: Exome sequencing was performed on three affected individuals from a single non-consanguineous family with presenting neurological abnormalities. The molecular consequences of the identified variant were evaluated by RNA analysis. Clinical features of the variant carriers were evaluated in detail. RESULTS: We identified a heterozygous dinucleotide deletion (c.2630-2_2630-1del) at the canonical acceptor splice site of MAPK8IP3. This variant co-segregated with the neurological phenotype in an affected mother and her two children. RNA analysis demonstrated that this variant leads to a partial deletion of exon 22 (r.2630_2673del), which is predicted to cause a frameshift and introduce a premature termination codon (p.Gly877Valfs∗36). Notably, despite carrying an identical genotype, the three affected individuals exhibited marked interindividual variability in clinical severity, ranging from mild specific learning difficulties to global developmental delay with severe intellectual disability and autism. CONCLUSION: This represents the first report of a familial, autosomal dominantly inherited pathogenic splice-site variant in MAPK8IP3, extending the established inheritance pattern beyond previously described de novo events. Our findings expand both the mutational and phenotypic spectrum of MAPK8IP3-related disorders, highlighting the complexity of genotype-phenotype correlations and underscoring the necessity of functional assays for accurate variant interpretation.

secondary.title: A toxic gain-of-function variant in MAPK8IP3 provides insights into JIP3 cellular roles.
secondary.abstract: Mitogen-activated protein kinase 8 interacting protein 3 (MAPK8IP3) gene encoding a protein called JIP3 is an adaption protein of the kinesin-1 complex known to play a role in axonal transport of cargo. Mutations in the gene have been linked to severe neurodevelopmental disorders, resulting in developmental delay, intellectual disability, ataxia, tremor, autism, seizures, and visual impairment. A patient who has a missense mutation in the MAPK8IP3 gene (c. 1714 C>T, Arg578Cys) (R578C) manifests dystonia, gross motor delay, and developmental delay. Here, we showed that the mutation was a toxic gain-of-function mutation that altered the interactome of JIP3; disrupted axonal transport of late endosomes; increased signaling via c-Jun N-terminal kinase, resulting in apoptosis; and disrupted dopamine receptor 1 signaling while not affecting dopamine receptor 2 signaling. Furthermore, in the presence of the mutant protein, we showed that an 80% reduction of mutant JIP3 and a 60% reduction of WT JIP3 by non-allele-selective phosphorothioate-modified antisense oligonucleotides was well tolerated by several types of cells in vitro. Our study identifies what we believe to be several important new roles for JIP3 and provides important insights for therapeutic approaches, including antisense oligonucleotide reduction of JIP3.

secondary.title: Comprehensive Clinical Characteristics, Longitudinal Adaptive Functioning, and Electroencephalogram Activity in MAPK8IP3-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder.
secondary.abstract: Mitogen-activated protein kinase 8-interacting protein 3-related neurodevelopmental disorder (MAPK8IP3-related NDD) results from heterozygous pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in MAPK8IP3. We report on 32 individuals (median age 7.5 years, range 1.3-22.0), all of whom had heterozygous pathogenic/likely pathogenic MAPK8IP3 variants, including missense (62.5%) and predicted loss-of-function (LOF) variants (34.4%). Common symptoms included cognitive impairment, hypotonia, motor difficulties, strabismus, microcephaly, and attention deficits. Corpus callosum thinning was reported in 62.1%. Nearly all individuals walked independently but demonstrated slower gait speed and a wider base of support compared to controls. The mean DAS-II General Conceptual Ability score was 62.5 ± 26.5. EEG analysis suggested a trend toward lower power accentuated frequency compared to typically developing individuals. Missense variants were associated with more severe symptoms than LOF variants. This study provides valuable insights into the clinical characteristics, patient management, and preparation for future clinical trials.

best.title: Insights into how JIP3 and JIP4 adaptor proteins relieve the auto-inhibited form of the kinesin-1 motor.
best.abstract: While our understanding of kinesin autoinhibition mechanisms is advancing, key insights into kinesin activation, especially autoinhibition relieved by cargo-motor adaptors, remain unclear. JIP3 and JIP4 are adaptors that activate kinesin-1 and dynein-dynactin motors, enabling bidirectional transport along microtubules. Here, we characterized the interaction between the kinesin-1 heavy chain, KIF5B, and both JIP3 and JIP4 (JIP3/4), using mutagenesis and binding experiments associated with modelling. We identified the minimal regions of JIP3/4 and KIF5B required for interaction. JIP3/4 binds to the CC4 coiled-coil domain of KIF5B, with no significant interaction detected with the distal tail. Conversely, KIF5B-CC4 binds to the RH1 domain of JIP3/4, with the preceding disordered N-terminus modulating the force of the binding. Notably, JIP3 and JIP4 exhibit ∼40-fold differences in affinity for KIF5B. We performed extensive site-directed mutagenesis on KIF5B-binding regions of JIP3/JIP4 targeting accessible charged residues and sequence differences between JIP3 and JIP4. This revealed multiple weak-affinity binding sites that collectively define an extensive KIF5B-binding surface on the RH1 domain of JIP3. Importantly, the KIF5B-binding surface on JIP3 differs from that of the DLIC (dynein light intermediate chain), confirming no competition between the two motors. Altogether, the fragment and mutant mapping of KIF5B binding to JIP3 and JIP4 presented here provides insights into how the auto-inhibited form of kinesin-1 might be relieved, with the CC4 region playing a central role.
best.authors: Vilela F, Chenon M, Campanacci V, Alik A, Velours C, Andreani J, Llinas P, Ménétrey J
best.overview: While our understanding of kinesin autoinhibition mechanisms is advancing, key insights into kinesin activation, especially autoinhibition relieved by cargo-motor adaptors, remain unclear.
best.main: We identified the minimal regions of JIP3/4 and KIF5B required for interaction.
limitations: We cannot exclude that other regions of JIP3/4 may also interact with kinesin-1 or that other factors are needed for full activation.

best.title: Ultrastructural studies reveal a new role for JIP3/MAPK8IP3 in endo-lysosomal maturation within the neuronal cell body.
best.abstract: In recent years, substantial heterogeneity in lysosomes, in terms of their composition, function, and positioning, has come to be recognized. Despite this, there are gaps in knowledge of our understanding of the molecular basis of lysosome heterogeneity, especially in neurons. To this end, we used electron microscopy to define endolysosomal organelles of human iPSC-derived neurons at the ultrastructural level. Through this, we identify endolysosomal maturation defects within neuronal cell bodies of iNeurons lacking JNK-Interacting Protein 3 (JIP3), a lysosome adaptor previously known to primarily regulate axonal lysosome movement. Loss of JIP3 results in an expansion of immature lysosomes within neuronal soma, along with a concomitant decrease in mature lysosomes. JIP3 loss also leads to delayed trafficking of endocytic cargo through these compartments, implicating JIP3 in the regulation of endolysosomal maturation within neuronal cell bodies. Our studies highlight the utility of electron microscopy in understanding neuronal lysosomal heterogeneity. Additionally, given recent links between JIP3 and a neurodevelopmental disorder, our findings here could provide new insight into mechanisms underlying neurodevelopmental pathology.

best.title: Characterization of a novel inherited splice-site variant in MAPK8IP3 expands the genetic and phenotypic spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders.
best.abstract: BACKGROUND: The MAPK8IP3 gene encodes JIP3, a kinesin-1 adapter protein crucial for axonal transport and JNK signaling pathway regulation. This gene exhibits extreme intolerance to loss-of-function variants. Heterozygous pathogenic MAPK8IP3 variants are linked to a neurodevelopmental disorder with or without variable brain abnormalities (NEDBA). This study characterizes a novel inherited canonical splice-site variant identified in a three-generation family. METHODS: Exome sequencing was performed on three affected individuals from a single non-consanguineous family with presenting neurological abnormalities. The molecular consequences of the identified variant were evaluated by RNA analysis. Clinical features of the variant carriers were evaluated in detail. RESULTS: We identified a heterozygous dinucleotide deletion (c.2630-2_2630-1del) at the canonical acceptor splice site of MAPK8IP3. This variant co-segregated with the neurological phenotype in an affected mother and her two children. RNA analysis demonstrated that this variant leads to a partial deletion of exon 22 (r.2630_2673del), which is predicted to cause a frameshift and introduce a premature termination codon (p.Gly877Valfs∗36). Notably, despite carrying an identical genotype, the three affected individuals exhibited marked interindividual variability in clinical severity, ranging from mild specific learning difficulties to global developmental delay with severe intellectual disability and autism. CONCLUSION: This represents the first report of a familial, autosomal dominantly inherited pathogenic splice-site variant in MAPK8IP3, extending the established inheritance pattern beyond previously described de novo events. Our findings expand both the mutational and phenotypic spectrum of MAPK8IP3-related disorders, highlighting the complexity of genotype-phenotype correlations and underscoring the necessity of functional assays for accurate variant interpretation.

best.title: A toxic gain-of-function variant in MAPK8IP3 provides insights into JIP3 cellular roles.
best.abstract: Mitogen-activated protein kinase 8 interacting protein 3 (MAPK8IP3) gene encoding a protein called JIP3 is an adaption protein of the kinesin-1 complex known to play a role in axonal transport of cargo. Mutations in the gene have been linked to severe neurodevelopmental disorders, resulting in developmental delay, intellectual disability, ataxia, tremor, autism, seizures, and visual impairment. A patient who has a missense mutation in the MAPK8IP3 gene (c. 1714 C>T, Arg578Cys) (R578C) manifests dystonia, gross motor delay, and developmental delay. Here, we showed that the mutation was a toxic gain-of-function mutation that altered the interactome of JIP3; disrupted axonal transport of late endosomes; increased signaling via c-Jun N-terminal kinase, resulting in apoptosis; and disrupted dopamine receptor 1 signaling while not affecting dopamine receptor 2 signaling. Furthermore, in the presence of the mutant protein, we showed that an 80% reduction of mutant JIP3 and a 60% reduction of WT JIP3 by non-allele-selective phosphorothioate-modified antisense oligonucleotides was well tolerated by several types of cells in vitro. Our study identifies what we believe to be several important new roles for JIP3 and provides important insights for therapeutic approaches, including antisense oligonucleotide reduction of JIP3.

best.title: JIP4 and RILPL1 utilize opposing motor force to dynamically regulate lysosomal tubulation.
best.abstract: Lysosomes are dynamic organelles that remodel their membrane in response to stimuli. We previously uncovered a process we term LYsosomal Tubulation/sorting driven by LRRK2 (LYTL), wherein damaged lysosomes generate tubules sorted into vesicles. LYTL is orchestrated by the Parkinson's disease kinase LRRK2 that recruits the motor adaptor protein and RHD family member JIP4 to lysosomes. JIP4 enhances LYTL tubule extension toward the plus-end of microtubules. To identify new players involved in LYTL, we mapped the lysosomal proteome after LRRK2 kinase inhibition. We found that RILPL1 is recruited to dysfunctional lysosomes in an LRRK2 kinase activity-dependent manner, facilitated by pRAB proteins. Unlike JIP4, RILPL1 induces retraction of LYTL tubules by binding to p150Glued, thereby moving lysosomal tubules toward the minus-end of microtubules. Our findings emphasize the dynamic regulation of LYTL tubules by two distinct RHD proteins and pRAB effectors, acting as opposing motor adaptor proteins. These opposing forces create a metastable lysosomal membrane deformation, enabling dynamic tubulation events.

best.title: Disruption of dynactin complex function in intellectual disability.
best.abstract: Intellectual disability (ID) is a highly prevalent condition affecting approximately 200 millions of people worldwide, characterized by impaired cognitive function. Dynactin complex consists of multiple protein subunits and is required for intracellular trafficking and synaptic homeostasis in developing and mature neurons. Here, we identify deleterious variants of dynactin subunit 4 (DCTN4) in ID pedigrees. DCTN4 ablation in mice results in altered neuronal positioning and apoptosis in neural progenitor cells. Notably, mice carrying the ID-linked DCTN4 variant exhibit cognitive deficits with impaired dendritic development. Cortical neurons with DCTN4 deficiency or variant show reduced levels of various dynactin subunits, suggesting that deficits in dynactin complex affects synaptic function. Furthermore, disruption of the DCTN4-JIP3 complex impairs lysosomal transport and dendritic development as well as synaptic development. Importantly, we showed that damaging variants in another dynactin subunit DCTN2 also disrupt neuronal positioning, reinforcing the critical role of dynactin complex in neurodevelopment and ID pathogenesis. These findings illustrate dysfunctional dynactin complex as a previously unrecognized disease mechanism of ID.

primary.title: BHLHE22 monoallelic and biallelic variants cause a neurodevelopmental disorder with agenesis of the corpus callosum, intellectual disability, abnormal muscle tone and movement abnormalities.
primary.abstract: BACKGROUND: BHLHE22 encodes a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor (bHLH) expressed exclusively in the retina and central nervous system (CNS), and functions as an important regulator of neuronal differentiation. However, BHLHE22 has not yet been associated with a Mendelian neurodevelopmental or neurological disorder. METHODS: Fifteen individuals from thirteen unrelated families carrying BHLHE22 variants identified by exome sequencing were collected through an international collaboration. RESULTS: De novo missense variants located in the highly conserved helix-loop-helix domain of the protein were found in six individuals, and one recurrent homozygous frameshift variant, NP_689627.1:p.Gly74AlafsTer18, was found in nine individuals. Frequent clinical features include absent or limited speech (10/13), delayed or impaired motor abilities (11/13), intellectual disability (9/12), partial or complete agenesis of the corpus callosum (12/15), involuntary movements and/or stereotypies (11/13), and abnormal muscle tone (13/13), depending on data availability. Two individuals developed spastic paraplegia, without intellectual disability (ID) or callosal anomalies. One individual had moderate developmental delay and ID, but without callosal anomalies. CONCLUSION: Collectively, our data establish BHLHE22 as a previously unrecognized neurodevelopmental disease gene. Disruption of BHLHE22, through either dominant or recessive variants, results in a distinct syndrome characterized by abnormalities in brain development, cognition, tone, and movement.

primary.title: Opposing Patterns of the Histone Variant MacroH2A1.1 in Fmr1 Knockout and BTBR T+ Itpr3tf/J Mouse Models of Autism Spectrum Disorder.
primary.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) exhibits substantial heterogeneity, wherein genetic and idiopathic forms may converge on shared core phenotypes through divergent molecular pathways. The histone variant macroH2A1.1, implicated in chromatin repression and DNA repair, has been linked to behavioral alterations opposite to core ASD features when depleted systemically. However, its regional and cell-type-specific regulation in genetic versus idiopathic ASD models remains unclear. We investigated macroH2A1.1 expression across the dorsal striatum, hippocampus, and medial prefrontal cortex in Fmr1 knockout (Fragile X syndrome model) and BTBR T+ Itpr3tf/J (idiopathic ASD model) mice. Quantitative PCR and imaging analyses revealed opposing patterns: BTBR mice showed region-specific mRNA downregulation and increased strongly stained macroH2A1.1-positive nuclei, whereas Fmr1 knockout mice exhibited reduced strong staining with increased weak staining, specific to neurons and not astrocytes, independent of significant mRNA changes. Bulk RNA-seq meta-analysis and pseudobulk single-cell transcriptomics further identified pathway-level enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation, chromatin remodeling, and transcriptional repression functional gene sets in unmatched public datasets (BTBR striatum; FXS hippocampus and cortex), with pronounced neuron-astrocyte divergence in Fmr1 knockout cortex. These findings underscore distinct epigenetic regulatory mechanisms in genetic and idiopathic ASD models.

primary.title: Maternal edible THC consumption alters offspring neurodevelopment and emotional behavior in rhesus macaques.
primary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Prenatal cannabis exposure is associated with adverse offspring outcomes including altered neurodevelopment. However, there is insufficient evidence to establish a direct association. We sought to determine the impact of chronic prenatal delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) exposure on offspring neurodevelopment and emotional behavior in a translational rhesus macaque model. METHODS: Animals were divided into two groups, control and THC-exposed, with both groups receiving a daily edible (placebo or THC) pre-conception, throughout pregnancy, and postnatally. MRI was performed longitudinally across gestation and infancy to assess volumetric and microstructural brain development. Serial behavioral testing, including motor and emotional assessments, was performed postnatally. At 6 months of age, brain tissue was collected for histology, immunohistochemistry (IHC), whole genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS), and bulk RNA-sequencing. FINDINGS: Analysis of the MRI images showed white matter changes with higher fractional anisotropy in the corpus callosum (CC) and centrum semiovale in THC-exposed infants. However, there were no significant differences in regional brain volumes. Behavioral testing demonstrated that THC-exposed infants displayed increased vocalizations and decreased independence. WGBS identified differentially methylated regions (DMRs) associated with THC exposure in the cerebellum and prefrontal cortex, annotated to genes involved in synaptic organization and brain development. RNA-sequencing confirmed differential expression of genes related to axon development and glutamatergic synapse, with expression correlating with methylation levels. INTERPRETATION: Chronic prenatal edible THC exposure in the rhesus macaque was associated with changes in white matter development, effects on infant behavior with signs of increased stress and anxiety, and brain DNA methylation and expression of genes involved in neurodevelopment. FUNDING: NIH, March of Dimes, Silver Family Innovation.

primary.title: Persistent neuronal stress signalling underlies Angelman syndrome phenotypes.
primary.abstract: Angelman syndrome is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder caused by the loss of UBE3A, a gene that encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase1,2. The mechanisms that underlie Angelman syndrome are not well understood, and in particular, the link between UBE3A substrates and disease phenotypes remains uncertain3. Here, using gain- and loss-of-function mutations in UBE3A4,5 along with unbiased proteomics, we show that asparagine synthetase (ASNS) is a target of UBE3A. We find that ASNS protein abundance is increased in the brains of Ube3a-null mice and in human neurons6. Genetic correction of ASNS overabundance rescues microcephaly and many behavioural deficits. Detailed molecular analyses show that ASNS overabundance activates stress signalling and causes a global reduction in neuronal protein synthesis. Our results suggest that loss of UBE3A traps neurons in a state of persistent stress and stunts neuronal growth during developmentally sensitive periods. Moreover, our results indicate that targeting ASNS and the stress response could hold therapeutic potential in Angelman syndrome.

primary.title: Domain-associated phenotypic patterns with MACF1 variants.
primary.abstract: PURPOSE: While heterozygous de novo missense variants in the microtubule-binding GAR domain of Microtubule-actin cross-linking factor 1 (MACF1) cause Lissencephaly 9 with Complex Brainstem Malformations (LIS9) [MIM 618325], the phenotypic impact of variants outside this domain remains unclear. METHODS: We assembled a cohort of 5 affected individuals from 4 unrelated families with biallelic non-GAR domain MACF1 variants who exhibit partially overlapping yet unique phenotypic traits. A sixth individual with a de novo, heterozygous frameshift variant was additionally identified. Combined with previously reported cases, we analyzed genotype and phenotype data from 22 individuals using Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO)-based unsupervised hierarchical clustering. RESULTS: Clustering revealed two distinct phenotypic signatures, suggesting domain-associated effects. Variants outside the GAR domain associate with broader neurodevelopmental phenotypes and craniofacial and skeletal involvement. Enrichment analysis (p < 0.001) using OMIM HPO sets supported these findings. In contrast to the GAR domain's strong correlation with LIS9, biallelic non-GAR domain MACF1 variants were linked to distinct developmental anomalies. CONCLUSION: These results expand the phenotypic spectrum of MACF1-related disorders and provide preliminary evidence for domain-associated MACF1 variant effects. While limited by sample size and lack of functional validation, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and underscore the utility of HPO-based clustering for systematic phenotype comparison as additional cases emerge. Comprehensive genetic and phenotypic assessments are essential for understanding the role of MACF1 in development, informing diagnosis, and guiding future research on cytoskeletal regulation in neurodevelopment.

primary.title: KATNAL2 dysfunction impairs microtubule dynamics and contributes to syndromic neurodevelopmental disease.
primary.abstract: Katanins are microtubule-severing ATPases. Dysfunction of katanin subunits has been implicated in impaired neurogenesis, morphogenesis, and neuronal migration. Although heterozygous variants in KATNAL2 (katanin-like 2), a known autism-spectrum disorder (ASD) risk gene, have been reported in patients with ASD or other neurodevelopmental disorders (NDD), the underlying cellular mechanisms remain incompletely defined. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) identified a homozygous missense variant in KATNAL2 (NM_001387690.1:c.1390T>C; p.(Ser464Pro)) in a pediatric patient presenting with severe global developmental delay, intellectual disability, infantile-onset epilepsy, and autistic features, extending the phenotypic spectrum beyond prior autism-focused associations. To elucidate the cellular mechanisms underlying KATNAL2 dysfunction, we established induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from patient fibroblasts and differentiated them into neural progenitor cells (NPCs) for quantitative immunofluorescence analyses of microtubule organization, microtubule regulatory proteins, and transcriptome profiling. In parallel, we generated CRISPR/Cas9 katnal2 zebrafish crispants and assessed body patterning and axonal projections using the transgenic nbt:dsRed line. Patient iPSC-derived NPCs showed impaired interphase microtubule network organization with increased angular standard deviation in directionality and mitotic/cytokinetic abnormalities, including abnormal positioning of the microtubule-rich cytokinetic midbody region. In vivo, CRISPR/Cas9 katnal2 zebrafish crispants showed abnormal body patterning together with disorganized motor neuron and posterior lateral line nerve axonal projections. Together, these findings support KATNAL2 as a regulator of microtubule network organization and mitotic progression in human NPCs. Our data from patient-derived NPCs and a zebrafish model provide functional evidence linking the p.(Ser464Pro) variant to an expanded syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotype.

primary.title: Overexpression of endoplasmic reticulum acetyl-CoA transporter AT-1 alters neuronal metabolism, growth, and synaptic activity.
primary.abstract: Acetyl-CoA is a molecule central to cellular metabolic homeostasis. As part of the secretory pathway, acetyl-CoA is imported into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by a membrane-bound transporter AT-1 (SLC33A1). AT-1 mutations have been linked to peripheral neuropathy, developmental delay with premature death, and intellectual disability with progeria. Here, we show that AT-1 overexpression impacts diverse phenotypes related to neuronal function and plasticity. Differences in ribosomal, synaptic processing, and metabolic pathways were identified at transcriptomic and proteomic levels. Metabolic adaptations included changes in mitochondrial membrane potential, architecture, and respiration, and tracing experiments revealed changes in the fate of glucose favoring glycogen storage over the pentose phosphate pathway. Altered redox was linked to NAD-dependent proteins SIRT1 and CtBP2. Depletion of lipid stores was associated with greater plasticity in fuel substrate utilization. Metabolic adaptation was coincident with decreased synaptic activity, indicating that neuronal communication is coordinated, in part, through acetyl-CoA metabolism.

primary.title: Evidence supporting the role of GIGYF2 in synapse development and autism.
primary.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a heterogeneous condition in which genetically defined subtypes offered insights into underlying biological mechanisms and potential targeted treatments. Here, we investigate the clinical and pathogenic significance of GIGYF2 variants in ASD through an integrated approach combining clinical genetics, conditional knockout (cKO) mouse models, neurobiology, and molecular studies. Through targeted sequencing, large-scale genomic data analysis of neurodevelopmental disorder cohorts, and international collaborations, we identified ten affected individuals from eight families harboring de novo or dominantly inherited likely gene-disruptive (LGD) variants and 13 affected individuals from 13 families with de novo missense variants in GIGYF2. Clinical characterization of 16 probands with GIGYF2 variants revealed common features, including ASD, language problems, intellectual disability, and anxiety. In a Gigyf2 cKO mouse model, we observed pronounced autistic-like behaviors, cognitive deficits, and anxiety-like behaviors, mirroring phenotypes observed in affected individuals. Mechanistically, Gigyf2 deficiency disrupted synaptic homeostasis, as evidenced by altered spine density and miniature excitatory postsynaptic currents, and impaired IGF-1R/mTOR signaling, along with dysregulation of synapse-related genes such as Nrp2. Pharmacological inhibition of mTOR with rapamycin or Torin1, as well as Nrp2 knockdown rescued synaptic defects in Gigyf2 KO neurons. These findings define a novel ASD subtype associated with GIGYF2 variants and establish GIGYF2 as a key regulator of synaptic development and function, implicating GIGYF2 dysfunction in ASD pathogenesis and highlighting the IGF-1R/mTOR pathway as a potential therapeutic target for GIGYF2-related ASD subtype.

primary.title: Disruption of dynactin complex function in intellectual disability.
primary.abstract: Intellectual disability (ID) is a highly prevalent condition affecting approximately 200 millions of people worldwide, characterized by impaired cognitive function. Dynactin complex consists of multiple protein subunits and is required for intracellular trafficking and synaptic homeostasis in developing and mature neurons. Here, we identify deleterious variants of dynactin subunit 4 (DCTN4) in ID pedigrees. DCTN4 ablation in mice results in altered neuronal positioning and apoptosis in neural progenitor cells. Notably, mice carrying the ID-linked DCTN4 variant exhibit cognitive deficits with impaired dendritic development. Cortical neurons with DCTN4 deficiency or variant show reduced levels of various dynactin subunits, suggesting that deficits in dynactin complex affects synaptic function. Furthermore, disruption of the DCTN4-JIP3 complex impairs lysosomal transport and dendritic development as well as synaptic development. Importantly, we showed that damaging variants in another dynactin subunit DCTN2 also disrupt neuronal positioning, reinforcing the critical role of dynactin complex in neurodevelopment and ID pathogenesis. These findings illustrate dysfunctional dynactin complex as a previously unrecognized disease mechanism of ID.

secondary.title: O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine homeostasis in brain health and disease: From physiology to neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders.
secondary.abstract: Protein O-GlcNAcylation is a dynamic and reversible post-translational modification that functions as a central nutrient-sensing mechanism linking cellular metabolism to protein function. Controlled by the opposing activities of O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine transferase and O-GlcNAcase, O-GlcNAcylation regulates thousands of nuclear, cytoplasmic, synaptic, and mitochondrial proteins involved in gene expression, neuronal differentiation, synaptic plasticity, proteostasis, mitochondrial homeostasis, and neuroimmune signaling. The brain exhibits particularly high O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine activity, reflecting its exceptional metabolic demands and the need to rapidly couple nutrient availability with neuronal function. Emerging evidence demonstrates that precise regulation of O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine cycling is indispensable throughout the lifespan, from embryonic neurodevelopment to healthy brain aging. Conversely, disruption of O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine homeostasis caused by genetic defects, metabolic disturbances, or environmental stress contributes to neurodevelopmental disorders. In the aging brain, impaired glucose metabolism and insulin resistance reduce O-GlcNAcylation, promoting mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, proteostasis failure, and the accumulation of pathogenic proteins. Consequently, dysregulated O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine signaling has emerged as a convergent mechanism underlying brain disorders spanning neurodevelopment to neurodegeneration. Although clinical translation remains challenging, growing evidence supports O-GlcNAcylation as a master regulator of brain homeostasis and a promising therapeutic target for neurological disorders. Collectively, this review highlights O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine signaling as a molecular bridge connecting early brain development, adulthood, and aging, providing an integrated framework for understanding brain physiology and disease.

secondary.title: Clinical, immunological and metabolic features and gut-brain axis markers in children with autism spectrum disorder and TORCH-associated central nervous system involvement.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorders (ASD) have heterogeneous etiologies, with TORCH infections potentially contributing to neurodevelopmental disruption through central nervous system injury and gut-brain axis dysfunction. METHODS: A prospective comparative study enrolled 280 children aged 3-10 years with ASD: 112 with TORCH-associated central nervous system (CNS) involvement (main group) and 168 with idiopathic ASD (comparison group), alongside 25 healthy controls. Assessments included clinical/neurological features, autism severity, gastrointestinal symptoms, pro-inflammatory cytokines, metabolic markers, neuron-specific enolase (NSE), fecal zonulin, and brain MRI. TORCH pathogens were detected by PCR from saliva samples. RESULTS: TORCH-associated ASD exhibited a more severe phenotype with greater frequencies of delayed speech, cognitive impairment, sleep disturbance, hyperactivity, emotional-behavioral dysregulation, epileptiform manifestations, and gastrointestinal symptoms. Severe ASD was significantly more common in the TORCH group. Laboratory analyses revealed significantly elevated interleukin-1β, interleukin-8, tumor necrosis factor alpha, homocysteine, ammonia, uric acid, NSE, and fecal zonulin, with reduced folate. Fecal zonulin was positively correlated with inflammatory markers and neuron-specific enolase. MRI more frequently demonstrated periventricular gliosis, ventriculomegaly, subependymal abnormalities, and diffuse residual organic changes. CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort, ASD with clinical evidence of TORCH-associated CNS involvement was associated with greater clinical severity and higher serum inflammatory, metabolic, neuronal-injury, fecal-zonulin, and structural MRI measures than ASD without such evidence. The cross-sectional design and limitations of salivary PCR preclude causal attribution to TORCH infection.

secondary.title: CNTN4: A Possible Candidate Gene for Microbiota-Gut-Brain Axis in Autism Spectrum Disorders and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder.
secondary.abstract: The gut microbiota plays a significant role in autism spectrum disorders (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), though findings vary substantially across studies. Using gut microbiome data from a genome-wide association study of 5,959 participants and summary statistics from 46,351 ASD and 55,374 ADHD cases, we conducted bidirectional Mendelian randomization (MR) analyses with inverse variance weighting as the primary method. Reverse MR analysis assessed potential reverse causality. We annotated single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) with SNP-nexus to identify associated genes, followed by Gene Ontology (﻿GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses to characterize their functional roles. Seventeen gut microbial taxa showed causal associations with ASD risk, while 27 were linked to ADHD. Reverse MR analysis revealed associations between aSD and species Desulfovibrio piger as well as species Bacillus U, but no reverse causality was detected for ADHD. Biological annotation identified five novel conserved genes in host-microbiome interactions shared by ASD and ADHD, with CNTN4 emerging as a common candidate gene. These findings support a potential causal relationship between gut microbiota and ASD/ADHD risk while uncovering novel conserved genes implicated in host-microbiome interactions for both disorders.Lay AbstractDistinct gut microbiota profiles were observed in individuals with ADHD and ASD. Seventeen microbial species showed significant associations with ASD, while 27 were linked to ADHD. secondary.title: Digital twin control framework uncovers individualized cross-scale links between functional connectivity deviations, communication impairment, and molecular mechanisms in autism.
secondary.abstract: BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is hallmarked by pronounced inter-individual heterogeneity in brain function and clinical manifestations. Conventional neuroimaging studies yield highly inconsistent findings, as extrinsic confounding factors and intrinsic disease heterogeneity mask ASD-specific functional connectivity (FC) signatures, hampering the identification of individualized neural mechanisms linked to symptom severity. METHODS: We developed a digital twin control analytical framework based on deep contrastive learning. By comparing each ASD participant with their matched digital twin control, we quantified individual-specific FC deviations. Principal component analysis was applied to extract the core aberrant pattern, followed by multi-dimensional analyzes and validation including clinical correlation, transcriptomic decoding, neurotransmitter and mitochondrial co-localization, as well as disease and cognitive enrichment. RESULTS: The model effectively disentangled disease‑related from non‑disease‑related variations. The identified dominant aberrant FC pattern was significantly associated with Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS) communication scores, suggesting it is associated with to communication impairment. This pattern showed convergent associations with synaptic pathways, excitatory/inhibitory neuronal signatures, critical developmental windows and subcortical structures, and exhibited negative spatial association with multiple neurotransmitter systems and mitochondrial respiratory complexes. Biological validation further supported its ASD specificity and communication‑related cognitive relevance. CONCLUSIONS: Leveraging the twin control analytical framework, this study provides an exploratory cross-scale framework linking individualized FC deviations with clinical, transcriptomic, neurochemical, and mitochondrial maps. The findings indicate that communication difficulties in ASD may partly arise from multi-scale disturbances in neural integration, social-perceptual processing and activity-dependent cellular energy regulation.

secondary.title: Characteristics of visual search and prefrontal brain activity in individuals with autism spectrum disorder: functional near-infrared spectroscopy study.
secondary.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The term 'visual search' (VS) is used to describe behaviors such as finding a desired item while shopping or looking for a room key. These behaviors are important in everyday life. Individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) have been reported to experience difficulties with VS. However, the characteristics of VS and the associated brain activity remain unclear. Therefore, we investigated these characteristics in detail using a measurement method that combined VS tasks with brain function measurements. METHODS: Twenty-one individuals with ASD and 42 typically developing (TD) individuals, matched for age and visual intelligence, participated in this study. The characteristics of VS were evaluated using two types of cancellation tasks: structured and random arrays. We evaluated VS performance using various measurements, including the rate of intersections and the best r, which reflect systematicity and directional constancy. We measured brain activity using functional near-infrared spectroscopy in the prefrontal cortex (PFC). RESULTS: The ASD group had a significantly higher rate of intersections and a significantly lower best r than the TD group. The right PFC activity was significantly higher than the activity in other PFC regions during the random array task in the TD group. Additionally, the TD group exhibited significantly higher right PFC activity than the ASD group. CONCLUSION: These results suggest that VS in individuals with ASD is characterized by inconsistent search direction and disorganization and that patterns of PFC brain activity during VS may also differ from those observed in TD individuals.

secondary.title: Attention Load Modulates Functional Brain Connectivity Reorganization in Children with High Autistic Traits: Evidence from Phase and Amplitude Coupling Metrics.
secondary.abstract: Whether emotional processing difficulties in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) stem from deficits in recognizing emotional stimuli or from limitations in flexibly reorganizing brain networks under increasing cognitive demands remains an open question. To our knowledge, this study is among the first to investigate the effects of graded attentional load (low/moderate/high) on EEG-based functional connectivity and brain network organization during task-irrelevant emotional prosody processing in children with high autistic traits (n = 31), by integrating phase-based (iPLV, wPLI) and amplitude-based (AEC) metrics together with graph-theoretic indices within a unified analytic framework. Connectivity matrices from a sliding-window approach were decomposed into edge-level, distributional, and graph-theoretic features and load-dependent changes in connectivity were assessed with statistical analyzes and classification models. The results suggested that attentional load did not uniformly increase or decrease connectivity but rather produced a multi-layered pattern of reorganization that varied as a function of frequency band, connectivity metric, and network topology. Phase-based connectivity in the beta band was decreased with increasing load, while amplitude envelope coupling (AEC) in the theta and alpha bands was increased under high load. This dual-mechanism pattern was most pronounced under the high-load condition, which yielded the greatest number of nominally significant features (uncorrected p<0.05; none survived FDR correction), the largest theta-AEC effect size (Kendall's W up to 0.22), and the best-performing classification model among those tested (accuracy = 72.6%, F1 = 0.725, AUC = 0.764). In conclusion, this exploratory study suggests that, in children with high autistic traits, increasing cognitive demands may be associated with band-specific network reorganization characterized by attenuated phase-based coordination alongside enhanced amplitude-based coupling; these patterns did not survive correction for multiple comparisons, have not been compared with those of typically developed children, and should be treated as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. If replicated, such findings could eventually inform how environmental stimulation and cognitive load are structured in special education settings.

secondary.title: WWOX-related developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (WOREE): A case series of seven patients from Argentina.
secondary.abstract: PURPOSE: WWOX-related developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (WOREE) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic WWOX variants, characterized by very early-onset epilepsy, profound developmental delay, and progressive brain abnormalities. Detailed electroclinical descriptions remain limited. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective study of seven patients with pathogenic/likely pathogenic WWOX variants. Clinical features, seizure evolution, EEG findings, brain MRI, and genetic data were reviewed. Epilepsy syndromes were classified according to International League against Epilepsy (ILAE) criteria. Variants were identified through next-generation sequencing and interpreted following American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) guidelines. RESULTS: Median seizure onset was 3 months (range 2-6). Five patients presented with focal seizures evolving to infantile epileptic spasms syndrome (IESS), while two had IESS at onset. Epilepsy was drug-resistant in all. Developmental delay was evident from birth with generalized hypotonia, acquired microcephaly, and impaired visual attention. Four patients had dysmorphic features. During the IESS period, EEG showed hypsarrhythmia in six patients and a severely disorganized encephalopathic background that did not strictly fulfill the criteria for hypsarrhythmia in one. Brain MRI revealed abnormalities in all patients, including frontotemporal atrophy and corpus callosum hypoplasia; delayed myelination was observed in one case. Eight pathogenic/likely pathogenic WWOX variants were found; including one novel variant (NM_016373.4:c.571C>T, p.(Gln191*)). The recurrent splice-site variant NM_016373.4:c.107+1G>A was identified in five patients, suggesting a possible regional founder effect. CONCLUSION: WOREE shows a recognizable electroclinical and neuroimaging profile with early drug-resistant epilepsy and profound developmental delay. Recognition of this pattern may facilitate early diagnosis and targeted genetic testing, particularly in populations with recurrent variants.

secondary.title: Conserved SINE and lineage-variable LINE-1 depletion at neurodevelopmental disorder promoters.
secondary.abstract: Developmental genes lie in transposon-poor regions, but whether that deficit is a conserved property of the promoters themselves remains unmeasured. Transposable element frequency was compared at neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) promoters (TSS ±2 kb) in seven primates and two outgroups, contrasting a curated NDD gene set (SFARI and ClinGen; [Formula: see text]) with brain-expressed housekeeping genes ([Formula: see text]). Alu depletion was significant in every primate ([Formula: see text] to [Formula: see text]), including the mouse lemur at 70 Mya. Mouse B1 and B2, SINEs amplified independently of primate Alu, each showed the deficit; the AT-biased Can-SINEs of dog did not. LINE-1 depletion was weak against housekeeping promoters but comparable to or deeper than the SINEs against the genome baseline, and more lineage-variable. The signal survived permutation testing, CpG and GC stratification, and gene-density and recombination controls. It persisted for alignment-defined rather than annotation-defined promoter windows, and against each genome's own baseline in seven of nine, marmoset and dog excepted; the squirrel monkey showed no such exception. Against human controls matched on constraint, brain expression and GC it narrowed but persisted ([Formula: see text]); Alu density does not otherwise track constraint. Windows away from the start site separate two components: the surrounding 250 kb is itself Alu-poor, and a promoter-proximal deficit survives normalisation to it. Depleted promoters coincided with active cis-regulatory elements, preferentially fetal-brain ones. Low promoter SINE content is thus an old feature of NDD-associated loci; whether the elements were never inserted or inserted and later lost is unresolved.

secondary.title: Biallelic SLC20A2 loss-of-function in severe early-onset neurodevelopmental disorder with brain calcification.
secondary.abstract: Biallelic SLC20A2 variants have recently been linked to a severe childhood-onset phenotype distinct from classical adult-onset primary brain calcification, but the molecular and radiologic consequences of homozygous truncating variants remain incompletely defined. We describe a child with severe early-onset neurodevelopmental disease caused by a homozygous SLC20A2 nonsense variant and provide clinical, neuroradiologic, segregation, and transcript-level characterization. The patient presented in early infancy with refractory seizures, severe hypotonia, left hemiplegia, profound developmental impairment, bilateral cataracts, and progressive intracranial calcification. Neuroimaging showed an unusual vascular and leptomeningeal calcification pattern with arterial narrowing, cytotoxic edema, subdural effusion, and rapid cerebral atrophy. Whole-exome sequencing identified a homozygous truncating variant, NM_001257180.2:c.1652 G > A, p.(Trp551Ter), in SLC20A2; both parents were heterozygous and showed radiologic findings consistent with SLC20A2-related primary brain calcification. RNA sequencing and RT-qPCR demonstrated marked reduction of SLC20A2 expression in patient-derived fibroblasts, supporting biallelic loss of function, whereas XPR1 expression was not significantly altered. Patient fibroblasts did not show overt Golgi fragmentation or ciliogenesis defects. These findings support a dose-dependent SLC20A2 disease spectrum and expand the phenotype associated with biallelic loss of function from primary brain calcification toward severe early-onset neurodevelopmental disorder with prominent vascular and leptomeningeal calcification.

secondary.title: Increased inflammatory cytokines in the temporal cortex in autism spectrum disorder.
secondary.abstract: Alterations in immune and neuroinflammatory processes are evident in neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorders (ASD). While prior studies using cerebrospinal fluid and plasma/serum have identified differences in cytokine levels in ASD when compared with controls, specific changes in postmortem human brain tissue remains poorly characterized. The superior temporal gyrus (STG) is involved in social communication and sensory processing, and is affected in ASD, making it a relevant region for investigating immune-related differences that has not been previously studied. Neuroimmune profiles were measured in STG tissue from 46 postmortem cases: ASD (n = 17), and neurotypical controls (n = 29). Fresh-frozen samples were collected using biopsy punches, and cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors were quantified using multiplexed bead immunoassays. In ASD cases, there were significantly increased levels of inflammatory cytokines in IL-1α, IL-8, IL-18, FLT-3L, FGF-2, G-CSF, M-CSF, MCP3, PDGF-AA and GROa compared to controls. In contrast, there was a significant decrease in RANTES, IFNα2 and IL-4 cytokine levels in ASD. Overall, ASD presented a distinctive STG cytokine profile with increased pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in the absence of an immune regulatory balance. These data highlights that unique neuroimmune pathways occur in neurodevelopmental disorders such as ASD offering insights into potential therapeutic targets.

secondary.title: Oscillatory Traveling Waves During Visual Entrainment in Autistic and Non-Autistic Adults.
secondary.abstract: Neural oscillations and traveling waves play a crucial role in cognition. In scalp electroencephalography (EEG), waves typically travel along the anterior-posterior axis: forward waves (occipital-to-frontal) predominate during sensory stimulation, while backward waves (frontal-to-occipital) emerge during rest and top-down modulation. Within the predictive coding framework, backward waves reflect predictive signals, whereas forward waves convey sensory processes and prediction errors. In this study, we investigated traveling wave dynamics during a visual entrainment task in non-autistic and autistic adults. Our results show an increase in backward waves during rhythmic visual stimulation in the non-autistic group, consistent with enhanced top-down predictions. Notably, we observed the opposite pattern in the autism group, characterized by a pronounced increase in forward waves at the entrained frequency (ω2 = 0.132). These results align with predictive coding accounts of autistic perception, which hypothesize a difference in balance between predictions and sensory evidence. Specifically, an increase in forward waves may reflect a bias toward sensory signaling over predictive feedback, due to atypical hierarchical communication across brain regions. Together, our findings shed new light on the oscillatory dynamics involved in visual entrainment in non-autistic adults and provide novel evidence in favor of predictive coding accounts of autistic perception.Lay AbstractThe brain continuously processes information by combining incoming sensory signals with prior expectations about the environment. According to predictive coding theories, perception depends on a balance between these two processes: the brain generates predictions about what is likely to happen and then updates those predictions when incoming sensory information does not match expectations. In autism, several theories suggest that this balance may be atypical, with perception relying more strongly on sensory input and less on prior predictions. One way to study how the brain communicates during perception is through 'traveling waves', patterns of rhythmic brain activity that move across the cortex over time. These waves can be measured noninvasively using electroencephalography (EEG). In visual tasks, waves traveling from the back of the brain toward the front are generally linked to the processing of sensory information, whereas waves traveling from the front toward the back are thought to reflect top-down signals such as predictions, expectations, and attentional control. In this study, we investigated traveling brain waves in autistic and non-autistic adults during a visual entrainment task, in which participants viewed rhythmic visual stimulation. We found that non-autistic participants showed an increase in backward traveling waves during stimulation, consistent with stronger predictive or top-down processing. In contrast, autistic participants showed the opposite pattern, with a marked increase in forward traveling waves at the frequency of the visual stimulation. This suggests a greater weighting of incoming sensory signals relative to predictive feedback in autism.

best.title: BHLHE22 monoallelic and biallelic variants cause a neurodevelopmental disorder with agenesis of the corpus callosum, intellectual disability, abnormal muscle tone and movement abnormalities.
best.abstract: BACKGROUND: BHLHE22 encodes a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor (bHLH) expressed exclusively in the retina and central nervous system (CNS), and functions as an important regulator of neuronal differentiation. However, BHLHE22 has not yet been associated with a Mendelian neurodevelopmental or neurological disorder. METHODS: Fifteen individuals from thirteen unrelated families carrying BHLHE22 variants identified by exome sequencing were collected through an international collaboration. RESULTS: De novo missense variants located in the highly conserved helix-loop-helix domain of the protein were found in six individuals, and one recurrent homozygous frameshift variant, NP_689627.1:p.Gly74AlafsTer18, was found in nine individuals. Frequent clinical features include absent or limited speech (10/13), delayed or impaired motor abilities (11/13), intellectual disability (9/12), partial or complete agenesis of the corpus callosum (12/15), involuntary movements and/or stereotypies (11/13), and abnormal muscle tone (13/13), depending on data availability. Two individuals developed spastic paraplegia, without intellectual disability (ID) or callosal anomalies. One individual had moderate developmental delay and ID, but without callosal anomalies. CONCLUSION: Collectively, our data establish BHLHE22 as a previously unrecognized neurodevelopmental disease gene. Disruption of BHLHE22, through either dominant or recessive variants, results in a distinct syndrome characterized by abnormalities in brain development, cognition, tone, and movement.

best.title: Opposing Patterns of the Histone Variant MacroH2A1.1 in Fmr1 Knockout and BTBR T+ Itpr3tf/J Mouse Models of Autism Spectrum Disorder.
best.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) exhibits substantial heterogeneity, wherein genetic and idiopathic forms may converge on shared core phenotypes through divergent molecular pathways. The histone variant macroH2A1.1, implicated in chromatin repression and DNA repair, has been linked to behavioral alterations opposite to core ASD features when depleted systemically. However, its regional and cell-type-specific regulation in genetic versus idiopathic ASD models remains unclear. We investigated macroH2A1.1 expression across the dorsal striatum, hippocampus, and medial prefrontal cortex in Fmr1 knockout (Fragile X syndrome model) and BTBR T+ Itpr3tf/J (idiopathic ASD model) mice. Quantitative PCR and imaging analyses revealed opposing patterns: BTBR mice showed region-specific mRNA downregulation and increased strongly stained macroH2A1.1-positive nuclei, whereas Fmr1 knockout mice exhibited reduced strong staining with increased weak staining, specific to neurons and not astrocytes, independent of significant mRNA changes. Bulk RNA-seq meta-analysis and pseudobulk single-cell transcriptomics further identified pathway-level enrichment of oxidative phosphorylation, chromatin remodeling, and transcriptional repression functional gene sets in unmatched public datasets (BTBR striatum; FXS hippocampus and cortex), with pronounced neuron-astrocyte divergence in Fmr1 knockout cortex. These findings underscore distinct epigenetic regulatory mechanisms in genetic and idiopathic ASD models.

best.title: Maternal edible THC consumption alters offspring neurodevelopment and emotional behavior in rhesus macaques.
best.abstract: BACKGROUND: Prenatal cannabis exposure is associated with adverse offspring outcomes including altered neurodevelopment. However, there is insufficient evidence to establish a direct association. We sought to determine the impact of chronic prenatal delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) exposure on offspring neurodevelopment and emotional behavior in a translational rhesus macaque model. METHODS: Animals were divided into two groups, control and THC-exposed, with both groups receiving a daily edible (placebo or THC) pre-conception, throughout pregnancy, and postnatally. MRI was performed longitudinally across gestation and infancy to assess volumetric and microstructural brain development. Serial behavioral testing, including motor and emotional assessments, was performed postnatally. At 6 months of age, brain tissue was collected for histology, immunohistochemistry (IHC), whole genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS), and bulk RNA-sequencing. FINDINGS: Analysis of the MRI images showed white matter changes with higher fractional anisotropy in the corpus callosum (CC) and centrum semiovale in THC-exposed infants. However, there were no significant differences in regional brain volumes. Behavioral testing demonstrated that THC-exposed infants displayed increased vocalizations and decreased independence. WGBS identified differentially methylated regions (DMRs) associated with THC exposure in the cerebellum and prefrontal cortex, annotated to genes involved in synaptic organization and brain development. RNA-sequencing confirmed differential expression of genes related to axon development and glutamatergic synapse, with expression correlating with methylation levels. INTERPRETATION: Chronic prenatal edible THC exposure in the rhesus macaque was associated with changes in white matter development, effects on infant behavior with signs of increased stress and anxiety, and brain DNA methylation and expression of genes involved in neurodevelopment.
