best.title: Effect of ALA on preventing diabetic peripheral neuropathy in rats through mitochondrial axonal transport.
best.abstract: PURPOSE: To explore the mechanism by which alpha-lipoic acid (ALA) regulates mitochondrial axonal transport to protect the sciatic nerve in diabetic rats. METHODS: Among 55 healthy male Sprague‒Dawley rats, 40 were randomly selected, fed a high-carbohydrate/high-fat diet and intraperitoneally injected with streptozotocin (STZ) to induce diabetes. Diabetic rats were randomly divided into diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN) and alpha lipoic acid (ALA) groups, with 15 rats in each group, excluding the rats in which diabetes failed to be induced and the dead rats. The other 15 rats were used as the control group. The rats in the ALA group were administered an ALA suspension (60 mg/kg/day) by gavage for 12 weeks. The rats in the control group and DPN group were gavaged with an equal volume of distilled water every day for 12 weeks. After the intervention was complete, the motor nerve conduction velocity (MNCV) and paw withdrawal threshold (PWT) were measured. Morphological changes in the sciatic nerve were observed by HE staining. Immunofluorescence staining and Western blotting were performed to measure protein expression levels. In vitro, a model of NSC34 cell injury was established by treating cells with high concentrations of glucose and palmitic acid sodium. NSC34 cells were randomly divided into the control group, DPN group and ALA group. The ALA group was treated with ALA for 24 hours. Changes in the axons of NSC34 cells were assessed by measuring the length of the axons. Immunofluorescence staining was performed to determine the fluorescence intensity of the cells, and Western blotting was performed to determine the grayscale value of each band. RESULTS: ALA increased the MNCV and PWT in DPN rats and increased the levels of phosphorylated AMP-activated protein kinase (p-AMPK) and phosphorylated cAMP-response element-binding protein (p-CREB). The expression of a motor protein involved in anterograde axonal mitochondrial transport, kinesin family member 5A (KIF5A), was upregulated, whereas the expression of a dynein protein involved in mitochondrial retrograde transport, Dynein cytoplasmic 1 intermediate chain 2 (DYNC1I2), was downregulated by ALA. CONCLUSION: The results of this study suggest that ALA alleviates peripheral nerve injury in diabetic rats by promoting the anterograde axonal transport of mitochondria, which may be related to AMPK/CREB signaling.

limitations: However, to date, the relationship between AMPK activation and DYNC1I2 expression has not been reported, and this relationship should be further explored in future studies.
However, ALA is mostly used for the short-term treatment of DPN, and future studies on the chronic efficacy and safety of α-lipoic acid are needed.

best.title: Genetic evidence for a functional association between Parkinson's disease proteins leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 and α-synuclein during axonal transport.
best.abstract: Mutations in α-synuclein (α-syn) and LRRK2 cause familial Parkinson's disease (fPD), yet how these proteins functionally interact remain ambiguous. We previously showed that α-syn undergoes bi-directional transport within axons and influences mitochondrial health, while other studies suggested that LRRK2-G2019S disrupts the axonal transport of autophagic vesicles and mitochondria. Here we tested the hypothesis that α-syn and LRRK2 are functionally linked during axonal transport. Expression of human LRRK2-WT in Drosophila larval nerves caused modest CSP-containing axonal blockages whereas no defects were seen in LRRK2 loss of function mutants in contrast to other proteins directly involved in axonal transport. Surprisingly, fPD mutations in the GTPase (LRRK2-Y1699C) and WD40 (LRRK2-G2385R) domains suppressed axonal blocks compared to LRRK2-WT, while kinase-domain mutant G2019S enhanced them. Reducing kinesin-1 had no effect with LRRK2-WT, but increased axonal transport defects with LRRK2-G2385R suggesting a functional interaction between the LRRK2 WD40 domain and the anterograde transport machinery. Further, co-expression of α-syn with either the GTPase domain or WD40 domain LRRK2 fPD mutants significantly suppressed α-syn-mediated axonal transport defects, decreased stalled α-syn-vesicles, but did not alter α-syn-mediated neuronal cell death. Taken together, these results suggest that while LRRK2 itself may not play an independent role in axonal transport, its GTPase and WD40 domains likely associate functionally with α-syn during transport within axons.

primary.title: Gαi2 promotes microtubule-driven incorporation of neurofilaments to stabilise nascent axons in vivo.
primary.abstract: Axon initiation is a critical step in the establishment of neuronal morphology. However, the mechanisms regulating stable axon initiation during embryonic development remain poorly understood. Here, using fixed-tissue super-resolution and high-resolution live-tissue imaging in the developing chick spinal cord, we reveal that stable axon initiation is characterised by microtubule-directed neurofilament accumulation in the emerging axon, and identify the multifunctional G-protein Gαi2 as a regulator of this process. Before axon initiation, microtubule network orientation shifts towards the site of the future axon where coiled Gαi2-associated neurofilaments accumulate asymmetrically before unfurling into the initiating axon behind microtubules. Crucially, Gαi2 is associated with neurofilaments and microtubules at their points of contact. Gαi2 depletion reduces engagement between these cytoskeletal networks and leads to impaired passage of neurofilaments into initiating axons and disrupted axon outgrowth, supporting a role for Gαi2 in regulating microtubule-driven incorporation of neurofilaments in nascent axons. These findings advance mechanistic understanding of polarity establishment and provide insight into cytoskeletal regulation during axon formation.

primary.title: The N-Ank protein Ankrd24 shapes neurons and couples to syndapin and the F-actin promoter Cobl-like.
primary.abstract: Proper neuromorphogenesis is pivotal for neuronal network formation and brain function. The underlying cell biological tasks are complex, as they include both remodeling of membrane topologies and of cytoskeletal structures. Yet, mechanisms coordinating these two different cell biological functions are largely unknown. Here, we molecularly and functionally characterize ankyrin repeat domain-containing protein 24 (Ankrd24) and demonstrate that this ankyrin-repeat protein is able to interact with and bend membranes and mechanistically and functionally belongs to the recently proposed N-Ank superfamily. Mutational analyses revealed that the N-Ank functions of Ankrd24 are indispensable for Ankrd24's role in neuromorphogenesis. Ankrd24 furthermore physically cooperated with the F-BAR domain protein syndapin I (PACSIN1) and with Cobl-like (Cobll1), a protein promoting actin filament formation, by ternary complex formation. Both partners were critical for Ankrd24-mediated dendritic arborization. This identified Ankrd24 as critical part of a larger, coordinated effort in inducing new dendritic branches. Our work thereby sheds light on the molecular mechanisms underlying the complex task of proper neuronal arbor development.

primary.title: KATNAL2 dysfunction impairs microtubule dynamics and contributes to syndromic neurodevelopmental disease.
primary.abstract: Katanins are microtubule-severing ATPases. Dysfunction of katanin subunits has been implicated in impaired neurogenesis, morphogenesis, and neuronal migration. Although heterozygous variants in KATNAL2 (katanin-like 2), a known autism-spectrum disorder (ASD) risk gene, have been reported in patients with ASD or other neurodevelopmental disorders (NDD), the underlying cellular mechanisms remain incompletely defined. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) identified a homozygous missense variant in KATNAL2 (NM_001387690.1:c.1390T>C; p.(Ser464Pro)) in a pediatric patient presenting with severe global developmental delay, intellectual disability, infantile-onset epilepsy, and autistic features, extending the phenotypic spectrum beyond prior autism-focused associations. To elucidate the cellular mechanisms underlying KATNAL2 dysfunction, we established induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from patient fibroblasts and differentiated them into neural progenitor cells (NPCs) for quantitative immunofluorescence analyses of microtubule organization, microtubule regulatory proteins, and transcriptome profiling. In parallel, we generated CRISPR/Cas9 katnal2 zebrafish crispants and assessed body patterning and axonal projections using the transgenic nbt:dsRed line. Patient iPSC-derived NPCs showed impaired interphase microtubule network organization with increased angular standard deviation in directionality and mitotic/cytokinetic abnormalities, including abnormal positioning of the microtubule-rich cytokinetic midbody region. In vivo, CRISPR/Cas9 katnal2 zebrafish crispants showed abnormal body patterning together with disorganized motor neuron and posterior lateral line nerve axonal projections. Together, these findings support KATNAL2 as a regulator of microtubule network organization and mitotic progression in human NPCs. Our data from patient-derived NPCs and a zebrafish model provide functional evidence linking the p.(Ser464Pro) variant to an expanded syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotype.

primary.title: Cross-species molecular mapping of the photoreceptor sensory cilium and periciliary structures identifies conserved and species-specific architectural features.
primary.abstract: Photoreceptor sensory cilia comprise a microtubule-based structural core and the phototransductive outer segment. The microtubule-based ciliary axoneme extends from the basal body through the connecting cilium into the outer segment, thereby linking the inner and outer segments. Around this central axis, specialized periciliary structures are distributed across the apical inner segment and basal outer segment. Yet how these ciliary and periciliary structures differ between rods and cones and across mammals remains incompletely defined. Using ultrastructure expansion microscopy, we compared their nanoscale molecular organization across canine, non-human primate and human retinas. Key rod-cone differences in ciliary organization were broadly conserved among all three species, whereas the scale and morphology of individual ciliary subcompartments differed between species. Periciliary structures showed even greater species-specific diversification, particularly in rods. Human photoreceptors shared several structural features with non-human primate photoreceptors but also displayed inter-individual variability in accessory inner segment-like structure. These findings refine current understanding of photoreceptor sensory cilia and associated periciliary structures in large mammals, revealing that conserved rod-cone differences co-exist with pronounced species-specific structural and molecular specializations.

primary.title: Kinesin-3 KIF1A functions as a diligent worker and its functionality is regulated by the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
primary.abstract: Long-distance intracellular transport is driven by motor proteins that walk along microtubule tracks. The fate of the motor protein after transport is unclear. Classically, motor proteins have been thought to function as Diligent Workers (DW) that remain attached to cargo during the entire transport event and are degraded at the end of the journey. In contrast, previous work suggests that kinesin-1 transport can be described by a Loose Bucket Brigade (LBB) model in which individual motor proteins participate in multiple rounds of transport. Here, we used live-cell imaging in iNeurons to test whether the kinesin-3 KIF1A functions as a DW during axonal transport. We demonstrate that the fluorescence intensity of KIF1A on particles undergoing axonal transport does not change over time, suggesting that KIF1A remains attached to its cargo for the entire transport event. We determined that KIF1A has a relatively short protein half-life, consistent with KIF1A being degraded at the end of the journey. Moreover, protein turnover appears to be tightly controlled in iNeurons, as treating cells with inhibitors of the ubiquitin/proteasome system results in a cessation of KIF1A-driven transport, the appearance of KIF1A aggregates in the cell body, and their subsequent degradation through aggrephagy. These results suggest that KIF1A transport fits the DW model and that KIF1A protein levels may play a role in signaling proteostatic stress in neuronal cells.

primary.title: Disruption of dynactin complex function in intellectual disability.
primary.abstract: Intellectual disability (ID) is a highly prevalent condition affecting approximately 200 millions of people worldwide, characterized by impaired cognitive function. Dynactin complex consists of multiple protein subunits and is required for intracellular trafficking and synaptic homeostasis in developing and mature neurons. Here, we identify deleterious variants of dynactin subunit 4 (DCTN4) in ID pedigrees. DCTN4 ablation in mice results in altered neuronal positioning and apoptosis in neural progenitor cells. Notably, mice carrying the ID-linked DCTN4 variant exhibit cognitive deficits with impaired dendritic development. Cortical neurons with DCTN4 deficiency or variant show reduced levels of various dynactin subunits, suggesting that deficits in dynactin complex affects synaptic function. Furthermore, disruption of the DCTN4-JIP3 complex impairs lysosomal transport and dendritic development as well as synaptic development. Importantly, we showed that damaging variants in another dynactin subunit DCTN2 also disrupt neuronal positioning, reinforcing the critical role of dynactin complex in neurodevelopment and ID pathogenesis. These findings illustrate dysfunctional dynactin complex as a previously unrecognized disease mechanism of ID.

primary.title: The postsynaptic scaffold protein ABLIM1 regulates seizure susceptibility by maintaining GluA2 membrane localization in chronic epilepsy.
primary.abstract: Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE), the most common form of drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) in adults, is a frequent chronic neurological disorder. Nevertheless, the precise pathophysiological mechanisms underlying TLE remain largely undefined. Our findings demonstrate that Actin-binding LIM protein 1 (ABLIM1) is broadly expressed in the adult mouse brain, with high expression in the hippocampus. The protein is primarily localized to neurons, enriched in the postsynaptic density (PSD), colocalizes with the scaffold protein PSD95, and directly binds to F-actin. Co-IP experiments confirmed that ABLIM1 interacts with the α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor (AMPAR) subunits GluA1 and GluA2. Following hippocampal stereotaxic injection of adeno-associated virus (AAV) to specifically knock down ABLIM1 expression, we observed reduced F-actin polymerization, decreased dendritic spine density, and thinning of the PSD in the mouse hippocampus. In the chronic epilepsy models induced by kainic acid (KA), ABLIM1 knockdown significantly exacerbated seizure severity and increased seizure susceptibility. Further mechanistic studies revealed that ABLIM1 knockdown specifically reduces membrane expression of GluA2 without altering its total protein levels. Collectively, ABLIM1 may regulate epileptogenesis and disease progression by maintaining postsynaptic structural integrity and GluA2 membrane homeostasis. Thus, the ABLIM1-GluA2 signaling axis represents a potential therapeutic target for DRE.

primary.title: Astrocyte SMN Restoration and Forskolin Treatment Improve SMA Synaptic Pathology.
primary.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Early phenotypic presentation of central afferent synapse dysfunction within patients with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) represents a key target for therapeutic development; however, the underlying disease mechanisms remain unresolved. By further investigating motor neuron synapse and peri-synaptic astrocyte process (PAP) defects in human SMA disease pathology, we aimed to develop a novel therapeutic approach to improve motor neuron function. METHODS: We utilized healthy subjects and patients with SMA induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cultures to assess phenotypes occurring intrinsically within astrocyte processes (monocultures) and at the PAP-synaptic interface (co-cultures), respectively, using cell surface capture mass spectrometry proteomics, confocal and super resolution microscopy, synaptogliosome (SG) isolation, and electrophysiology. RESULTS: SMA astrocytes demonstrated intrinsic filopodia actin defects featuring low abundance of actin-associated cell surface N-glycoproteins, decreased filopodia density and CDC42-GTP levels after actin remodeling stimulation, and significantly reduced phosphorylated ezrin, radixin, and moesin (pERM) proteins. Within the SMA motor neuron and astrocyte co-cultures, we observed concurrent decreases in synapse number, actin-associated synapsin I expression, and PAP-associated expression of pERM proteins. Our dual treatment paradigm using SMN1 gene therapy combined with forskolin treatment to stimulate actin dynamics via increasing cyclic adenosine monophosphate levels resulted in increased branching and filopodia density of SMA astrocytes, and improved synapse formation and function of SMA motor neurons. INTERPRETATION: We define actin-associated defects impacting astrocyte filopodia dynamics and motor neuron synaptic function in SMA. This shaped our therapeutic approach targeted to SMN-dependent and actin-related disease mechanisms, which overall demonstrated improvements in motor neuron function and disease pathology. ANN NEUROL 2026.

primary.title: KIF1A c.773C > T impairs neural progenitor differentiation and axonal transport in association with dysregulated Wnt/β-catenin-BDNF signaling.
primary.abstract: Pathogenic KIF1A variants are established cause neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders. However, the mechanisms by which they perturb early human neural development remains undefined. Here, we identified a heterozygous KIF1A c.773C > T (p.T258M) mutation in a Chinese family with hereditary spastic paraplegia and modeled its pathogenicity using patient-derived iPSCs and CRISPR-Cas9-corrected isogenic controls. We found that KIF1A-mutant neural stem cells (NSCs) exhibited hyperproliferation, impaired cell-cycle exit, and defective neuronal differentiation, accompanied by defective neurite outgrowth, neuronal complexity, and calcium activity. Mechanistically, the KIF1A c.773C > T mutation compromised the binding affinity of KIF1A for β-tubulin and thereby impaired microtubule-associated localization of BDNF and synaptophysin. Integrated transcriptomic and biochemical analyses further revealed dysregulation of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway. Notably, pharmacological activation of Wnt signaling restored BDNF expression, whereas exogenous BDNF rescued the proliferative and differentiative defects, indicating a potential functional relationship between BDNF and Wnt/β-catenin signaling. Collectively, these findings suggested that dysregulated Wnt/β-catenin-BDNF signaling may serve as a contributory mechanism linking KIF1A motor dysfunction to aberrant neural stem cell fate.

primary.title: Pathogenic KIF1A variants differentially disrupt axonal trafficking and impede synaptic development.
primary.abstract: The nervous system relies on billions of neurons connected through trillions of synapses to support vital functions. Despite the importance of this synaptic network, cellular mechanisms dictating synapse formation during human neurodevelopment remain unclear. Long-distance trafficking by the microtubule motor KIF1A is crucial for synaptogenesis and downstream synapse maintenance. Mutations in KIF1A cause KIF1A-associated neurological disorder (KAND). We employed isogenic gene-edited human-induced pluripotent stem cell -derived neurons to assess the effects of disparate pathogenic mutations in KIF1A on synaptic trafficking and function. Null (p.C92*) and hypoactive (p.P305L) mutations delay neurite outgrowth, mislocalize synaptic cargoes, and decrease synapse density. Conversely, a hyperactive (p.R350G) mutation supports neurite outgrowth but causes aberrant motility of synaptic vesicle precursors and deficits in microtubule-dependent presynaptic patterning. Functional analysis of neuronal activity reveals delayed synaptic maturation in loss-of-function mutations (p.P305L, p.C92*) and precocious activity in the hyperactive p.R350G mutation. These data provide insights into how KIF1A mutations with distinct molecular-level impacts lead to significant downstream synaptic deficits in human neurons.

primary.title: EGR1 mediates neuronal damage via suppressing HIF1A-induced mitophagy following traumatic brain injury.
primary.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains a leading cause of neurological morbidity and mortality, characterized by complex pathophysiological cascades. Here, we investigate the role of the transcription factor EGR1 (early growth response 1) in modulating mitochondrial homeostasis via the HIF1A (hypoxia inducible factor 1, alpha subunit)-BNIP3 (BCL2/adenovirus E1B interacting protein 3) axis following TBI. Using integrated transcriptomic and epigenomic analyses, we identified EGR1 as a critical regulator of TBI pathology, with its expression acutely upregulated in neurons post-injury. Genetic ablation of Egr1 in mice significantly reduced neuronal apoptosis, preserved dendritic integrity, and ameliorated cognitive and sensorimotor deficits. Mechanistically, chromatin immunoprecipitation and luciferase assays revealed that EGR1 directly binds to the Hif1a promoter, repressing its transcription. Loss of EGR1 enhanced HIF1A-BNIP3-mediated mitophagy, reducing mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress both in vitro and in vivo. Conversely, silencing HIF1A or BNIP3 abrogated the neuroprotective effects of EGR1 deficiency. secondary.title: Postsynaptic remodeling and F-actin dysregulation in the Dctn1Δ2-4 mouse model of motor neuron disease.
secondary.abstract: The microtubule motor dynein and its co-adaptor dynactin govern organelle positioning within highly polarized neurons. The dynactin subunit p150Glued, encoded by DCTN1, is associated with motor neuron disease. The p150Glued G59S mutation disrupts the microtubule-binding domain and drives selective motor neuron degeneration in patients and animal models. The p150Glued microtubule-binding domain mediates the initiation of retrograde transport at axonal terminals and stabilizes presynaptic sites at neuromuscular junctions. Nevertheless, the key functions of p150Glued and its microtubule-binding domain within postsynaptic compartments remain poorly defined. Using Dctn1Δ2-4 mice, in which exons 2-4 of Dctn1 encoding the microtubule-binding domain are deleted, we performed morphological, biochemical, and cellular physiological analyses, together with genetic manipulation and pharmacological intervention, to investigate how loss of p150Glued microtubule-binding function affects excitatory postsynaptic organization and neuronal vulnerability. We found that excitatory postsynaptic remodeling occurred before overt dendritic degeneration and motor neuron loss in Dctn1Δ2-4 mice. We further demonstrated that p150Glued microtubule-binding domain dysfunction induced early remodeling of excitatory postsynaptic densities, leading to increased postsynaptic accumulation of N-methyl- D-aspartate receptors, dysregulated Ca2+ homeostasis, and heightened susceptibility to glutamate-induced excitotoxicity. Mechanistically, p150Glued microtubule-binding domain dysfunction promoted the postsynaptic accumulation of endosomes and the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and SCAR homolog complex, resulting in excessive F-actin assembly and pathological enhancement of postsynaptic density architecture. Furthermore, these postsynaptic abnormalities were rescued by re-expression of wild-type p150Glued, but not the disease-associated G59S mutant. Pharmacological inhibition of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors, in turn, attenuated excitotoxic injury and neurodegeneration. Our findings identify a previously unrecognized postsynaptic pathogenic mechanism in DCTN1-associated motor neuron disease. secondary.title: Neurofilament transport kinetics can be explained by the activity of small numbers of independent kinesin and dynein motors.
secondary.abstract: Neurofilaments, which are intermediate filaments, are long flexible protein polymers that are transported bidirectionally along microtubule tracks in axons. Kymograph analysis of neurofilaments has revealed rapid intermittent movement with average run lengths consistent with the processive bouts of single motors, and frequent pauses and reversals that suggest rapid switching between opposing motors. To explore this, we used discrete stochastic models of kinesin and dynein motors to simulate neurofilament movement by teams of independent motors in axons. We describe an unbiased automated sampling algorithm to identify the numbers of kinesin and dynein motors required to match the range of pause times, run times, run lengths, and velocities for neurofilaments in a large data set of ∼37,000 runs and pauses acquired with 30.3 ms resolution. We find that the diverse kinetic behavior of neurofilaments can be explained by the activity of 1-2 kinesin or dynein motors, which interact indirectly via the mechanical forces they exert on the neurofilament cargo. Simultaneous engagement of opposing motors was rare in our simulations, indicating that the motile behavior can be explained by alternating kinesin and dynein activity without a competition between motors of opposite directionality.

secondary.title: PIST couples actin cytoskeleton dynamics through a WH2-like actin-binding domain.
secondary.abstract: Purkinje cell synapses in the cerebellar cortex require tight coordination between receptor trafficking and cytoskeletal remodeling to sustain synaptogenesis, structural plasticity, and motor learning. The glutamate δ2 receptor (GluRδ2), a hallmark component of parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapses, depends on intracellular scaffolding proteins for proper localization and signaling. PIST (GOPC), a neuronal PDZ domain-containing protein originally identified as a selective GluRδ2-interacting partner, has emerged as an important regulator of receptor trafficking and synaptic organization. Here, we reveal a previously unrecognized biochemical function of PIST as an actin-binding protein. Biochemical and cellular analyses show that PIST directly associates with filamentous actin in a concentration-dependent manner, suppresses actin polymerization in vitro, and co-localizes with actin in neuronal cells. Mechanistically, this interaction is mediated by a WH2-like motif within PIST. PIST may function as a molecular link between the actin cytoskeleton and the protein trafficking machinery, suggesting a potential new mechanism underlying the coordinated regulation of receptor transport and synaptic structural plasticity in neurons.

secondary.title: Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6)-mediated α-tubulin (K40) deacetylation and microtubule destabilization disrupt autophagosome-lysosome fusion in PBDE-47-induced neurotoxicity.
secondary.abstract: 2,2',4,4'-tetrabromodiphenyl ether (PBDE-47) is a pervasive environmental brominated flame retardant that accumulates in nervous tissues and induces persistent neurotoxicity. Emerging evidence indicates that PBDE-47 perturbs neuronal autophagy, yet the definitive upstream molecular mechanism remains uncharacterized, hindering the development of effective protective strategies. This study was performed to clarify the toxic regulatory cascade and explore feasible pharmacological interventions using in vivo neonatal rat hippocampal tissue and in vitro PC12 neuronal cell models. Animals were neonatally exposed to PBDE-47 (0.1, 1.0, 10.0 mg/kg·bw), and PC12 cells were treated with PBDE-47 (1, 10, 20 µM) for mechanistic exploration. Results showed that PBDE-47 dose-dependently upregulated histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6), decreased α-tubulin (K40) acetylation, and destabilized neuronal microtubules. Such microtubule structural damage impaired autophagosome retrograde trafficking, blocked autophagosome-lysosome fusion, and eventually caused neuronal loss, synaptic protein reduction, and cognitive impairment. For mechanism validation and rescue experiments, 1 mg/kg·bw paclitaxel (PTX) and 1 mg/kg·bw tubastatin A (TBA) were administered to neonatal rats, whereas 12.5 nmol/L PTX and 10 µmol/L TBA were used for PC12 cell treatment to stabilize microtubules and selectively inhibit HDAC6, respectively. Both pharmacological interventions effectively restored tubulin acetylation, rescued defective autophagic flux, and mitigated PBDE-47-induced neuronal injury, with TBA showing better applicability due to its high blood-brain barrier permeability and biosafety. Behavioral tests in vivo verified that PTX and TBA treatment significantly ameliorated PBDE-47-elicited learning and memory deficits. Collectively, these findings define the HDAC6/microtubule acetylation axis as a core upstream pathway responsible for PBDE-47-triggered autophagic transport failure and neurotoxicity, providing robust experimental evidence and a promising therapeutic target for the prevention of PBDEs-mediated neurological disorders.

secondary.title: Suppression of Tau-tubulin kinase 1 mitigates tau phosphorylation, and Aβ mediated neurotoxicity via altered kinase network.
secondary.abstract: Tau-tubulin kinase-1 (TTBK1) is a neuron-specific serine/threonine tau kinase that is highly expressed in the entorhinal and hippocampal regions and phosphorylates microtubule-associated protein tau at sites relevant to Alzheimer's disease (AD), thereby contributing to early tau pathology. Targeting TTBK1 can be a promising therapeutic approach for AD, although how suppression of TTBK1 may change neuronal functions is poorly understood. Here we show the proteome and phosphoproteome analysis of murine primary cortical neurons transduced with adeno-associated virus (AAV) expressing short hairpin RNA (shRNA) targeting murine Ttbk1, using tandem mass tag and data independent acquisition liquid chromatography/mass-spectrometry. Suppression of TTBK1 expression by shRNA transduction increases expression of neuronal intermediate filament proteins and V1-domain subunits of the vacuolar H+-ATPase, suggesting the regulatory roles of TTBK1 on cytoskeletal dynamics and lysosomal activity. Silencing of Ttbk1 significantly reduces phosphorylation of TTBK1 and MAP1A as well as increases phosphorylation of neuronal intermediate filament proteins, indicating the regulation of microtubule-related proteins and axonal stabilization. Phosphosite-specific signature analysis identifies the kinases regulated by TTBK1 including AD-related cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (CDK5) and AKT1. Silencing of Ttbk1 significantly reduces CDK5 activator p25/p35 ratio and pT231 phospho-tau level, consistent with the reduced activity of CDK5. Finally, silencing of Ttbk1 reduces amyloid-β-induced neurotoxicity in vitro. These results suggest a close functional relationship or coordinated regulation among TTBK1 and other kinases in maintaining axonal homeostasis via phosphorylation of microtubule-associated proteins, and mediating amyloid-β toxicity, thus emphasize TTBK1 as an emerging therapeutic target of AD.

secondary.title: Microtubule and cytoskeletal destabilization gene expression in the brain vasculature after experimental diffuse traumatic brain injury: Implications for neurodegenerative disease later in life.
secondary.abstract: Neurodegenerative disease risk following traumatic brain injury (TBI) has been associated with vascular abnormalities and brain inflammation. However, the extent to which diffuse TBI with at least one persistent neurological deficit contributes to chronic neurodegeneration is not well understood. In this study, we investigated the impact of experimental diffuse TBI on the cerebral vasculature in the CA1 region of the hippocampus, which is vulnerable to multiple cognitive-associated neurodegenerative diseases. At 6-months post-injury, a timepoint with known cognitive impairment, we employed laser capture microdissection (LCM) to isolate parenchymal blood vessels from the CA1 subregion of the hippocampus in Sprague-Dawley rats subjected to either sham or midline fluid percussion injury. LCM vessels were processed for RNA sequencing and differentially expressed gene (DEG) analyses (DESeq2) were performed, followed by pathway enrichment analysis using genes with a log2FC > 0 and p-value < 0.05. A subset of differentially expressed genes (9%) were associated with microtubule/cytoskeletal organization, including the PLEC gene (encoding plectin) (Log2FC=+9.5, p < 0.0001), a cytoskeletal protein that maintains tissue integrity and whose overexpression has recently been identified as a risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD). Pathway analyses showed the most upregulated and downregulated biological pathways were involved in neurodegeneration-multiple-diseases (Gene count 11, p-adjusted < 0.01) and AD (Gene count 8, p-adjusted < 0.04). Understanding the complex interplay between TBI, the cerebral vasculature, and neurodegeneration risk is critical for prognosis and interventions that mitigate the long-term effects of brain injury and improve outcomes for patients.

secondary.title: Elevation of the mechanically-sensitive e protein emerin links nuclear mechanotransduction to tau-induced cytoskeletal remodeling in neurons.
secondary.abstract: Neurodegenerative tauopathies, including Alzheimer's disease, are neuropathologically defined by pathological tau deposition. While tau drives neurotoxicity by disrupting cytoskeletal, nucleoskeletal, and genomic architecture, cellular mechanisms mediating tau-induced dysfunction of the cytoskeleton and nucleoskeleton are incompletely understood. Here, we identify proteins with differing abundance in a cellular tauopathy model, iTau. Building upon previous findings that pathogenic tau reduces nuclear tension, we find elevated levels of emerin, a central regulator of nuclear mechanotransduction, in iTau neurons and tau mutant iPSC-derived neurons. Neuronal emerin overexpression drives neurotoxicity, increases filamentous actin (F-actin), and induces nuclear invagination, mimicking cellular phenotypes of tauopathy. Alterations in emerin binding partners reflect its cytosolic relocalization in iTau neurons, suggesting that pathogenic tau may impact nuclear mechanotransduction by altering emerin levels and localization. Overall, we identify emerin as a potential mediator of cytoskeletal and nucleoskeletal remodeling in tauopathy and provide a foundation for future studies of emerin function in neurons.

best.title: Gαi2 promotes microtubule-driven incorporation of neurofilaments to stabilise nascent axons in vivo.
best.abstract: Axon initiation is a critical step in the establishment of neuronal morphology. However, the mechanisms regulating stable axon initiation during embryonic development remain poorly understood. Here, using fixed-tissue super-resolution and high-resolution live-tissue imaging in the developing chick spinal cord, we reveal that stable axon initiation is characterised by microtubule-directed neurofilament accumulation in the emerging axon, and identify the multifunctional G-protein Gαi2 as a regulator of this process. Before axon initiation, microtubule network orientation shifts towards the site of the future axon where coiled Gαi2-associated neurofilaments accumulate asymmetrically before unfurling into the initiating axon behind microtubules. Crucially, Gαi2 is associated with neurofilaments and microtubules at their points of contact. Gαi2 depletion reduces engagement between these cytoskeletal networks and leads to impaired passage of neurofilaments into initiating axons and disrupted axon outgrowth, supporting a role for Gαi2 in regulating microtubule-driven incorporation of neurofilaments in nascent axons. These findings advance mechanistic understanding of polarity establishment and provide insight into cytoskeletal regulation during axon formation.

best.title: The N-Ank protein Ankrd24 shapes neurons and couples to syndapin and the F-actin promoter Cobl-like.
best.abstract: Proper neuromorphogenesis is pivotal for neuronal network formation and brain function. The underlying cell biological tasks are complex, as they include both remodeling of membrane topologies and of cytoskeletal structures. Yet, mechanisms coordinating these two different cell biological functions are largely unknown. Here, we molecularly and functionally characterize ankyrin repeat domain-containing protein 24 (Ankrd24) and demonstrate that this ankyrin-repeat protein is able to interact with and bend membranes and mechanistically and functionally belongs to the recently proposed N-Ank superfamily. Mutational analyses revealed that the N-Ank functions of Ankrd24 are indispensable for Ankrd24's role in neuromorphogenesis. Ankrd24 furthermore physically cooperated with the F-BAR domain protein syndapin I (PACSIN1) and with Cobl-like (Cobll1), a protein promoting actin filament formation, by ternary complex formation. Both partners were critical for Ankrd24-mediated dendritic arborization. This identified Ankrd24 as critical part of a larger, coordinated effort in inducing new dendritic branches. Our work thereby sheds light on the molecular mechanisms underlying the complex task of proper neuronal arbor development.

best.title: Postsynaptic remodeling and F-actin dysregulation in the Dctn1Δ2-4 mouse model of motor neuron disease.
best.abstract: The microtubule motor dynein and its co-adaptor dynactin govern organelle positioning within highly polarized neurons. The dynactin subunit p150Glued, encoded by DCTN1, is associated with motor neuron disease. The p150Glued G59S mutation disrupts the microtubule-binding domain and drives selective motor neuron degeneration in patients and animal models. The p150Glued microtubule-binding domain mediates the initiation of retrograde transport at axonal terminals and stabilizes presynaptic sites at neuromuscular junctions. Nevertheless, the key functions of p150Glued and its microtubule-binding domain within postsynaptic compartments remain poorly defined. Using Dctn1Δ2-4 mice, in which exons 2-4 of Dctn1 encoding the microtubule-binding domain are deleted, we performed morphological, biochemical, and cellular physiological analyses, together with genetic manipulation and pharmacological intervention, to investigate how loss of p150Glued microtubule-binding function affects excitatory postsynaptic organization and neuronal vulnerability. We found that excitatory postsynaptic remodeling occurred before overt dendritic degeneration and motor neuron loss in Dctn1Δ2-4 mice. We further demonstrated that p150Glued microtubule-binding domain dysfunction induced early remodeling of excitatory postsynaptic densities, leading to increased postsynaptic accumulation of N-methyl- D-aspartate receptors, dysregulated Ca2+ homeostasis, and heightened susceptibility to glutamate-induced excitotoxicity. Mechanistically, p150Glued microtubule-binding domain dysfunction promoted the postsynaptic accumulation of endosomes and the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and SCAR homolog complex, resulting in excessive F-actin assembly and pathological enhancement of postsynaptic density architecture. Furthermore, these postsynaptic abnormalities were rescued by re-expression of wild-type p150Glued, but not the disease-associated G59S mutant. Pharmacological inhibition of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors, in turn, attenuated excitotoxic injury and neurodegeneration. Our findings identify a previously unrecognized postsynaptic pathogenic mechanism in DCTN1-associated motor neuron disease. We propose that loss of p150Glued microtubule-binding function disrupts postsynaptic endosome positioning, leading to aberrant Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein and SCAR homolog-mediated F-actin remodeling, pathological enhancement of excitatory postsynaptic densities, excessive N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor targeting, and increased vulnerability to excitotoxicity.

best.title: KATNAL2 dysfunction impairs microtubule dynamics and contributes to syndromic neurodevelopmental disease.
best.abstract: Katanins are microtubule-severing ATPases. Dysfunction of katanin subunits has been implicated in impaired neurogenesis, morphogenesis, and neuronal migration. Although heterozygous variants in KATNAL2 (katanin-like 2), a known autism-spectrum disorder (ASD) risk gene, have been reported in patients with ASD or other neurodevelopmental disorders (NDD), the underlying cellular mechanisms remain incompletely defined. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) identified a homozygous missense variant in KATNAL2 (NM_001387690.1:c.1390T>C; p.(Ser464Pro)) in a pediatric patient presenting with severe global developmental delay, intellectual disability, infantile-onset epilepsy, and autistic features, extending the phenotypic spectrum beyond prior autism-focused associations. To elucidate the cellular mechanisms underlying KATNAL2 dysfunction, we established induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from patient fibroblasts and differentiated them into neural progenitor cells (NPCs) for quantitative immunofluorescence analyses of microtubule organization, microtubule regulatory proteins, and transcriptome profiling. In parallel, we generated CRISPR/Cas9 katnal2 zebrafish crispants and assessed body patterning and axonal projections using the transgenic nbt:dsRed line. Patient iPSC-derived NPCs showed impaired interphase microtubule network organization with increased angular standard deviation in directionality and mitotic/cytokinetic abnormalities, including abnormal positioning of the microtubule-rich cytokinetic midbody region. In vivo, CRISPR/Cas9 katnal2 zebrafish crispants showed abnormal body patterning together with disorganized motor neuron and posterior lateral line nerve axonal projections. Together, these findings support KATNAL2 as a regulator of microtubule network organization and mitotic progression in human NPCs. Our data from patient-derived NPCs and a zebrafish model provide functional evidence linking the p.(Ser464Pro) variant to an expanded syndromic neurodevelopmental phenotype.

best.title: Cross-species molecular mapping of the photoreceptor sensory cilium and periciliary structures identifies conserved and species-specific architectural features.
best.abstract: Photoreceptor sensory cilia comprise a microtubule-based structural core and the phototransductive outer segment. The microtubule-based ciliary axoneme extends from the basal body through the connecting cilium into the outer segment, thereby linking the inner and outer segments. Around this central axis, specialized periciliary structures are distributed across the apical inner segment and basal outer segment. Yet how these ciliary and periciliary structures differ between rods and cones and across mammals remains incompletely defined. Using ultrastructure expansion microscopy, we compared their nanoscale molecular organization across canine, non-human primate and human retinas. Key rod-cone differences in ciliary organization were broadly conserved among all three species, whereas the scale and morphology of individual ciliary subcompartments differed between species. Periciliary structures showed even greater species-specific diversification, particularly in rods. Human photoreceptors shared several structural features with non-human primate photoreceptors but also displayed inter-individual variability in accessory inner segment-like structure. These findings refine current understanding of photoreceptor sensory cilia and associated periciliary structures in large mammals, revealing that conserved rod-cone differences co-exist with pronounced species-specific structural and molecular specializations.

best.title: Kinesin-3 KIF1A functions as a diligent worker and its functionality is regulated by the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
best.abstract: Long-distance intracellular transport is driven by motor proteins that walk along microtubule tracks. The fate of the motor protein after transport is unclear. Classically, motor proteins have been thought to function as Diligent Workers (DW) that remain attached to cargo during the entire transport event and are degraded at the end of the journey. In contrast, previous work suggests that kinesin-1 transport can be described by a Loose Bucket Brigade (LBB) model in which individual motor proteins participate in multiple rounds of transport. Here, we used live-cell imaging in iNeurons to test whether the kinesin-3 KIF1A functions as a DW during axonal transport. We demonstrate that the fluorescence intensity of KIF1A on particles undergoing axonal transport does not change over time, suggesting that KIF1A remains attached to its cargo for the entire transport event. We determined that KIF1A has a relatively short protein half-life, consistent with KIF1A being degraded at the end of the journey. Moreover, protein turnover appears to be tightly controlled in iNeurons, as treating cells with inhibitors of the ubiquitin/proteasome system results in a cessation of KIF1A-driven transport, the appearance of KIF1A aggregates in the cell body, and their subsequent degradation through aggrephagy. These results suggest that KIF1A transport fits the DW model and that KIF1A protein levels may play a role in signaling proteostatic stress in neuronal cells.

best.title: Disruption of dynactin complex function in intellectual disability.
best.abstract: Intellectual disability (ID) is a highly prevalent condition affecting approximately 200 millions of people worldwide, characterized by impaired cognitive function. Dynactin complex consists of multiple protein subunits and is required for intracellular trafficking and synaptic homeostasis in developing and mature neurons. Here, we identify deleterious variants of dynactin subunit 4 (DCTN4) in ID pedigrees. DCTN4 ablation in mice results in altered neuronal positioning and apoptosis in neural progenitor cells. Notably, mice carrying the ID-linked DCTN4 variant exhibit cognitive deficits with impaired dendritic development. Cortical neurons with DCTN4 deficiency or variant show reduced levels of various dynactin subunits, suggesting that deficits in dynactin complex affects synaptic function. Furthermore, disruption of the DCTN4-JIP3 complex impairs lysosomal transport and dendritic development as well as synaptic development. Importantly, we showed that damaging variants in another dynactin subunit DCTN2 also disrupt neuronal positioning, reinforcing the critical role of dynactin complex in neurodevelopment and ID pathogenesis. These findings illustrate dysfunctional dynactin complex as a previously unrecognized disease mechanism of ID.

best.title: The postsynaptic scaffold protein ABLIM1 regulates seizure susceptibility by maintaining GluA2 membrane localization in chronic epilepsy.
best.abstract: Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE), the most common form of drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE) in adults, is a frequent chronic neurological disorder. Nevertheless, the precise pathophysiological mechanisms underlying TLE remain largely undefined. Our findings demonstrate that Actin-binding LIM protein 1 (ABLIM1) is broadly expressed in the adult mouse brain, with high expression in the hippocampus. The protein is primarily localized to neurons, enriched in the postsynaptic density (PSD), colocalizes with the scaffold protein PSD95, and directly binds to F-actin. Co-IP experiments confirmed that ABLIM1 interacts with the α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptor (AMPAR) subunits GluA1 and GluA2. Following hippocampal stereotaxic injection of adeno-associated virus (AAV) to specifically knock down ABLIM1 expression, we observed reduced F-actin polymerization, decreased dendritic spine density, and thinning of the PSD in the mouse hippocampus. In the chronic epilepsy models induced by kainic acid (KA), ABLIM1 knockdown significantly exacerbated seizure severity and increased seizure susceptibility. Further mechanistic studies revealed that ABLIM1 knockdown specifically reduces membrane expression of GluA2 without altering its total protein levels. Collectively, ABLIM1 may regulate epileptogenesis and disease progression by maintaining postsynaptic structural integrity and GluA2 membrane homeostasis. Thus, the ABLIM1-GluA2 signaling axis represents a potential therapeutic target for DRE.

We describe an unbiased automated sampling algorithm to identify the numbers of kinesin and dynein motors required to match the range of pause times, run times, run lengths, and velocities for neurofilaments in a large data set of ∼37,000 runs and pauses acquired with 30.3 ms resolution. We find that the diverse kinetic behavior of neurofilaments can be explained by the activity of 1-2 kinesin or dynein motors, which interact indirectly via the mechanical forces they exert on the neurofilament cargo. Simultaneous engagement of opposing motors was rare in our simulations, indicating that the motile behavior can be explained by alternating kinesin and dynein activity without a competition between motors of opposite directionality.

best.title: Astrocyte SMN Restoration and Forskolin Treatment Improve SMA Synaptic Pathology.
best.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Early phenotypic presentation of central afferent synapse dysfunction within patients with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) represents a key target for therapeutic development; however, the underlying disease mechanisms remain unresolved. By further investigating motor neuron synapse and peri-synaptic astrocyte process (PAP) defects in human SMA disease pathology, we aimed to develop a novel therapeutic approach to improve motor neuron function. METHODS: We utilized healthy subjects and patients with SMA induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cultures to assess phenotypes occurring intrinsically within astrocyte processes (monocultures) and at the PAP-synaptic interface (co-cultures), respectively, using cell surface capture mass spectrometry proteomics, confocal and super resolution microscopy, synaptogliosome (SG) isolation, and electrophysiology. RESULTS: SMA astrocytes demonstrated intrinsic filopodia actin defects featuring low abundance of actin-associated cell surface N-glycoproteins, decreased filopodia density and CDC42-GTP levels after actin remodeling stimulation, and significantly reduced phosphorylated ezrin, radixin, and moesin (pERM) proteins. Within the SMA motor neuron and astrocyte co-cultures, we observed concurrent decreases in synapse number, actin-associated synapsin I expression, and PAP-associated expression of pERM proteins. Our dual treatment paradigm using SMN1 gene therapy combined with forskolin treatment to stimulate actin dynamics via increasing cyclic adenosine monophosphate levels resulted in increased branching and filopodia density of SMA astrocytes, and improved synapse formation and function of SMA motor neurons. INTERPRETATION: We define actin-associated defects impacting astrocyte filopodia dynamics and motor neuron synaptic function in SMA. This shaped our therapeutic approach targeted to SMN-dependent and actin-related disease mechanisms, which overall demonstrated improvements in motor neuron function and disease pathology. best.title: PIST couples actin cytoskeleton dynamics through a WH2-like actin-binding domain.
best.abstract: Purkinje cell synapses in the cerebellar cortex require tight coordination between receptor trafficking and cytoskeletal remodeling to sustain synaptogenesis, structural plasticity, and motor learning. The glutamate δ2 receptor (GluRδ2), a hallmark component of parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synapses, depends on intracellular scaffolding proteins for proper localization and signaling. PIST (GOPC), a neuronal PDZ domain-containing protein originally identified as a selective GluRδ2-interacting partner, has emerged as an important regulator of receptor trafficking and synaptic organization. Here, we reveal a previously unrecognized biochemical function of PIST as an actin-binding protein. Biochemical and cellular analyses show that PIST directly associates with filamentous actin in a concentration-dependent manner, suppresses actin polymerization in vitro, and co-localizes with actin in neuronal cells. Mechanistically, this interaction is mediated by a WH2-like motif within PIST. PIST may function as a molecular link between the actin cytoskeleton and the protein trafficking machinery, suggesting a potential new mechanism underlying the coordinated regulation of receptor transport and synaptic structural plasticity in neurons.

best.title: Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6)-mediated α-tubulin (K40) deacetylation and microtubule destabilization disrupt autophagosome-lysosome fusion in PBDE-47-induced neurotoxicity.
best.abstract: 2,2',4,4'-tetrabromodiphenyl ether (PBDE-47) is a pervasive environmental brominated flame retardant that accumulates in nervous tissues and induces persistent neurotoxicity. Emerging evidence indicates that PBDE-47 perturbs neuronal autophagy, yet the definitive upstream molecular mechanism remains uncharacterized, hindering the development of effective protective strategies. This study was performed to clarify the toxic regulatory cascade and explore feasible pharmacological interventions using in vivo neonatal rat hippocampal tissue and in vitro PC12 neuronal cell models. Animals were neonatally exposed to PBDE-47 (0.1, 1.0, 10.0 mg/kg·bw), and PC12 cells were treated with PBDE-47 (1, 10, 20 µM) for mechanistic exploration. Results showed that PBDE-47 dose-dependently upregulated histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6), decreased α-tubulin (K40) acetylation, and destabilized neuronal microtubules. Such microtubule structural damage impaired autophagosome retrograde trafficking, blocked autophagosome-lysosome fusion, and eventually caused neuronal loss, synaptic protein reduction, and cognitive impairment. For mechanism validation and rescue experiments, 1 mg/kg·bw paclitaxel (PTX) and 1 mg/kg·bw tubastatin A (TBA) were administered to neonatal rats, whereas 12.5 nmol/L PTX and 10 µmol/L TBA were used for PC12 cell treatment to stabilize microtubules and selectively inhibit HDAC6, respectively. Both pharmacological interventions effectively restored tubulin acetylation, rescued defective autophagic flux, and mitigated PBDE-47-induced neuronal injury, with TBA showing better applicability due to its high blood-brain barrier permeability and biosafety. Behavioral tests in vivo verified that PTX and TBA treatment significantly ameliorated PBDE-47-elicited learning and memory deficits. Collectively, these findings define the HDAC6/microtubule acetylation axis as a core upstream pathway responsible for PBDE-47-triggered autophagic transport failure and neurotoxicity, providing robust experimental evidence and a promising therapeutic target for the prevention of PBDEs-mediated neurological disorders.

best.title: Suppression of Tau-tubulin kinase 1 mitigates tau phosphorylation, and Aβ mediated neurotoxicity via altered kinase network.
best.abstract: Tau-tubulin kinase-1 (TTBK1) is a neuron-specific serine/threonine tau kinase that is highly expressed in the entorhinal and hippocampal regions and phosphorylates microtubule-associated protein tau at sites relevant to Alzheimer's disease (AD), thereby contributing to early tau pathology. Targeting TTBK1 can be a promising therapeutic approach for AD, although how suppression of TTBK1 may change neuronal functions is poorly understood. Here we show the proteome and phosphoproteome analysis of murine primary cortical neurons transduced with adeno-associated virus (AAV) expressing short hairpin RNA (shRNA) targeting murine Ttbk1, using tandem mass tag and data independent acquisition liquid chromatography/mass-spectrometry. Suppression of TTBK1 expression by shRNA transduction increases expression of neuronal intermediate filament proteins and V1-domain subunits of the vacuolar H+-ATPase, suggesting the regulatory roles of TTBK1 on cytoskeletal dynamics and lysosomal activity. Silencing of Ttbk1 significantly reduces phosphorylation of TTBK1 and MAP1A as well as increases phosphorylation of neuronal intermediate filament proteins, indicating the regulation of microtubule-related proteins and axonal stabilization. Phosphosite-specific signature analysis identifies the kinases regulated by TTBK1 including AD-related cyclin-dependent kinase 5 (CDK5) and AKT1. Silencing of Ttbk1 significantly reduces CDK5 activator p25/p35 ratio and pT231 phospho-tau level, consistent with the reduced activity of CDK5. Finally, silencing of Ttbk1 reduces amyloid-β-induced neurotoxicity in vitro. These results suggest a close functional relationship or coordinated regulation among TTBK1 and other kinases in maintaining axonal homeostasis via phosphorylation of microtubule-associated proteins, and mediating amyloid-β toxicity, thus emphasize TTBK1 as an emerging therapeutic target of AD.

best.title: KIF1A c.773C > T impairs neural progenitor differentiation and axonal transport in association with dysregulated Wnt/β-catenin-BDNF signaling.
best.abstract: Pathogenic KIF1A variants are established cause neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders. However, the mechanisms by which they perturb early human neural development remains undefined. Here, we identified a heterozygous KIF1A c.773C > T (p.T258M) mutation in a Chinese family with hereditary spastic paraplegia and modeled its pathogenicity using patient-derived iPSCs and CRISPR-Cas9-corrected isogenic controls. We found that KIF1A-mutant neural stem cells (NSCs) exhibited hyperproliferation, impaired cell-cycle exit, and defective neuronal differentiation, accompanied by defective neurite outgrowth, neuronal complexity, and calcium activity. Mechanistically, the KIF1A c.773C > T mutation compromised the binding affinity of KIF1A for β-tubulin and thereby impaired microtubule-associated localization of BDNF and synaptophysin. Integrated transcriptomic and biochemical analyses further revealed dysregulation of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway. Notably, pharmacological activation of Wnt signaling restored BDNF expression, whereas exogenous BDNF rescued the proliferative and differentiative defects, indicating a potential functional relationship between BDNF and Wnt/β-catenin signaling. Collectively, these findings suggested that dysregulated Wnt/β-catenin-BDNF signaling may serve as a contributory mechanism linking KIF1A motor dysfunction to aberrant neural stem cell fate.

best.title: Pathogenic KIF1A variants differentially disrupt axonal trafficking and impede synaptic development.
best.abstract: The nervous system relies on billions of neurons connected through trillions of synapses to support vital functions. Despite the importance of this synaptic network, cellular mechanisms dictating synapse formation during human neurodevelopment remain unclear. Long-distance trafficking by the microtubule motor KIF1A is crucial for synaptogenesis and downstream synapse maintenance. Mutations in KIF1A cause KIF1A-associated neurological disorder (KAND). We employed isogenic gene-edited human-induced pluripotent stem cell -derived neurons to assess the effects of disparate pathogenic mutations in KIF1A on synaptic trafficking and function. Null (p.C92*) and hypoactive (p.P305L) mutations delay neurite outgrowth, mislocalize synaptic cargoes, and decrease synapse density. Conversely, a hyperactive (p.R350G) mutation supports neurite outgrowth but causes aberrant motility of synaptic vesicle precursors and deficits in microtubule-dependent presynaptic patterning. Functional analysis of neuronal activity reveals delayed synaptic maturation in loss-of-function mutations (p.P305L, p.C92*) and precocious activity in the hyperactive p.R350G mutation. These data provide insights into how KIF1A mutations with distinct molecular-level impacts lead to significant downstream synaptic deficits in human neurons.

best.title: Microtubule and cytoskeletal destabilization gene expression in the brain vasculature after experimental diffuse traumatic brain injury: Implications for neurodegenerative disease later in life.
best.abstract: Neurodegenerative disease risk following traumatic brain injury (TBI) has been associated with vascular abnormalities and brain inflammation. However, the extent to which diffuse TBI with at least one persistent neurological deficit contributes to chronic neurodegeneration is not well understood. In this study, we investigated the impact of experimental diffuse TBI on the cerebral vasculature in the CA1 region of the hippocampus, which is vulnerable to multiple cognitive-associated neurodegenerative diseases. At 6-months post-injury, a timepoint with known cognitive impairment, we employed laser capture microdissection (LCM) to isolate parenchymal blood vessels from the CA1 subregion of the hippocampus in Sprague-Dawley rats subjected to either sham or midline fluid percussion injury. LCM vessels were processed for RNA sequencing and differentially expressed gene (DEG) analyses (DESeq2) were performed, followed by pathway enrichment analysis using genes with a log2FC > 0 and p-value < 0.05. A subset of differentially expressed genes (9%) were associated with microtubule/cytoskeletal organization, including the PLEC gene (encoding plectin) (Log2FC=+9.5, p < 0.0001), a cytoskeletal protein that maintains tissue integrity and whose overexpression has recently been identified as a risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD). Pathway analyses showed the most upregulated and downregulated biological pathways were involved in neurodegeneration-multiple-diseases (Gene count 11, p-adjusted < 0.01) and AD (Gene count 8, p-adjusted < 0.04). Understanding the complex interplay between TBI, the cerebral vasculature, and neurodegeneration risk is critical for prognosis and interventions that mitigate the long-term effects of brain injury and improve outcomes for patients.

best.title: EGR1 mediates neuronal damage via suppressing HIF1A-induced mitophagy following traumatic brain injury.
best.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) remains a leading cause of neurological morbidity and mortality, characterized by complex pathophysiological cascades. Here, we investigate the role of the transcription factor EGR1 (early growth response 1) in modulating mitochondrial homeostasis via the HIF1A (hypoxia inducible factor 1, alpha subunit)-BNIP3 (BCL2/adenovirus E1B interacting protein 3) axis following TBI. Using integrated transcriptomic and epigenomic analyses, we identified EGR1 as a critical regulator of TBI pathology, with its expression acutely upregulated in neurons post-injury. Genetic ablation of Egr1 in mice significantly reduced neuronal apoptosis, preserved dendritic integrity, and ameliorated cognitive and sensorimotor deficits. Mechanistically, chromatin immunoprecipitation and luciferase assays revealed that EGR1 directly binds to the Hif1a promoter, repressing its transcription. Loss of EGR1 enhanced HIF1A-BNIP3-mediated mitophagy, reducing mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress both in vitro and in vivo. Conversely, silencing HIF1A or BNIP3 abrogated the neuroprotective effects of EGR1 deficiency. best.title: Elevation of the mechanically-sensitive e protein emerin links nuclear mechanotransduction to tau-induced cytoskeletal remodeling in neurons.
best.abstract: Neurodegenerative tauopathies, including Alzheimer's disease, are neuropathologically defined by pathological tau deposition. While tau drives neurotoxicity by disrupting cytoskeletal, nucleoskeletal, and genomic architecture, cellular mechanisms mediating tau-induced dysfunction of the cytoskeleton and nucleoskeleton are incompletely understood. Here, we identify proteins with differing abundance in a cellular tauopathy model, iTau. Building upon previous findings that pathogenic tau reduces nuclear tension, we find elevated levels of emerin, a central regulator of nuclear mechanotransduction, in iTau neurons and tau mutant iPSC-derived neurons. Neuronal emerin overexpression drives neurotoxicity, increases filamentous actin (F-actin), and induces nuclear invagination, mimicking cellular phenotypes of tauopathy. Alterations in emerin binding partners reflect its cytosolic relocalization in iTau neurons, suggesting that pathogenic tau may impact nuclear mechanotransduction by altering emerin levels and localization. Overall, we identify emerin as a potential mediator of cytoskeletal and nucleoskeletal remodeling in tauopathy and provide a foundation for future studies of emerin function in neurons.

primary.title: An integrated human forebrain organoid reveals microglia-mediated CD8+ T cell recruitment and neuroimmune dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease pathology.
primary.abstract: Genetic evidence implicates immune dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the neuroimmune mechanisms operating in human tissue remain poorly defined. Here, we establish a modular human forebrain organoid platform that systematically integrates human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived microglia and CD8+ T cells to reconstitute multicellular AD pathology. This system enables functional interrogation of both innate and adaptive immune components in a human-relevant context. Using this platform, we demonstrate that microglia mediate amyloid-β clearance and neuronal maturation but also drive inflammatory activation and recruit CD8+ T cells through CCL4/5 signaling via CCR1/5 and CXCR3, establishing a neuroinflammatory feedback loop. Pharmacological targeting of CCR5 or CXCR3 blocks T cell recruitment and modulates autophagy in a microglia-dependent manner. This modular organoid platform provides a versatile tool for dissecting neuron-immune interactions and enables cell-type-specific therapeutic screening in human neuroinflammatory disease models.

primary.title: Cas9 nickase-mediated contraction of CAG/CTG repeats is associated with phenotypic improvements in a Huntington's disease mouse model.
primary.abstract: Expanded CAG/CTG repeats cause more than 15 different diseases that all remain without a disease-modifying treatment. Because repeat length accounts for most of the variation in disease severity, contracting CAG/CTG repeats presents an attractive therapeutic avenue. Here, we show that the CRISPR-Cas9 nickase targeted to CAG/CTG repeats leads to efficient repeat contractions in Huntington's disease (HD) patient-derived neurons and astrocytes and in myotonic dystrophy type 1 patient-derived neurons. The approach was allele selective and free of detectable off-target mutations. Injection of the Cas9 nickase into the striatum of the R6/1 mouse model of HD using adeno-associated viral vectors led to repeat contractions in more than half of striatal neurons. Upon injection, we observed a reduction in the number of inclusion bodies, an improved gene expression profile, and amelioration of locomotion deficits in the open field test. The effects were greater than expected from the contractions induced, suggesting that non-cell autonomous mechanisms may be involved. Our results provide the proof of concept that correction of CAG/CTG repeats can improve HD phenotypes in a mouse disease model.

primary.title: OGT regulates RNA-binding protein nucleocytoplasmic partitioning, but this fails in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
primary.abstract: O-linked N-acetylglucosamine transferase (OGT) catalyzes the O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) modification to proteins and has been implicated in a range of diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a rapidly progressive and currently incurable neurodegenerative disorder. However, the precise mechanisms by which OGT influences ALS pathogenesis remain largely unresolved. In this study, we used human-induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived spinal motor neurons (hiPSC-MNs), the principal cell type that undergoes degeneration in ALS, to systematically reveal that OGT-related mechanisms regulate RNA-binding protein (RBP) nucleocytoplasmic compartmentalization. Using a combination of antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) technology and small molecular pharmacology, we reveal two distinct regulatory mechanisms of RBP compartmentalization, including by intron-retaining transcript-mediated sequestration and O-linked N-acetylglucosaminylation (O-GlcNAcylation)-mediated nuclear transport. We finally examine the tractability of manipulating OGT activity in the ALS context but demonstrate that the OGT-related mechanisms governing RBP localization in healthy hiPSC-MNs are impaired in the context of ALS-causing VCP and TARDBP mutations.

primary.title: VPS13A loss of function mutations cause disruption of cellular calcium homeostasis and increase the vulnerability to ferroptosis.
primary.abstract: VPS13A belongs to the family of bridge-like lipid transfer proteins, which connect opposing membranes at organelle contact sites in order to facilitate bulk lipid transfer. Loss of function mutations in the VPS13A gene cause VPS13A disease. Diminished store operated calcium entry has previously been described in patient-derived fibroblasts and iPSC-derived neurons from VPS13A disease patients and impairments in mitochondrial calcium uptake was observed in patient-derived fibroblasts. However, how calcium (dys)homeostasis is regulated and its effects on neuronal survival remain enigmatic. Here, we investigated calcium regulation and cell death in induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons from VPS13A disease patients. We demonstrate that reduced store operated calcium entry is associated with diminished plasma membrane-ER contact sites and altered expression of the calcium release-activated calcium channel ORAI1. VPS13A-deficient neurons further exhibited elevated mitochondrial calcium levels, as well as resistance of the mitochondrial calcium uniporter to inhibition by Ru360. Further, VPS13A disease neurons show increased lipid peroxidation, driving ferroptotic cell death. These findings establish a mechanistic link between disrupted calcium homeostasis and neuronal degeneration in VPS13A disease and identify calcium (dys)homeostasis and ferroptosis as potential pathogenic pathways and therapeutic targets.

primary.title: KIF1A-Mediated Axonal Transport of Netrin-1 in iPSC-Derived Human Forebrain Neurons.
primary.abstract: Netrin-1 is a secreted laminin-like protein that functions as a guidance cue for axon pathfinding in development. Netrin-1 also modulates synapse formation in developing neurons and long-term potentiation in mature neurons. Netrin-1 is expressed in human neurons; however, its intracellular distribution and trafficking have not been assessed. Moreover, there is a genetic association in Caenorhabditis elegans between UNC-6/netrin-1 and UNC-104/KIF1A, a kinesin-3 motor protein required for axonal transport. We characterized the endogenous expression of netrin-1 via immunocytochemistry and demonstrated it is localized to both the axon and dendrites of induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived human forebrain neurons. Next, live-cell imaging of netrin-1-mRFP revealed rapid, bidirectional axonal transport, comparable to that of other cargos undergoing microtubule-based trafficking in vertebrate neurons. Finally, we demonstrated a role for the kinesin-3 motor protein, KIF1A, in Netrin-1 transport by demonstrating that KIF1A-associated neurological disease (KAND) patient variants significantly reduce netrin-1 axonal transport.

primary.title: Pathogenic KIF1A variants differentially disrupt axonal trafficking and impede synaptic development.
primary.abstract: The nervous system relies on billions of neurons connected through trillions of synapses to support vital functions. Despite the importance of this synaptic network, cellular mechanisms dictating synapse formation during human neurodevelopment remain unclear. Long-distance trafficking by the microtubule motor KIF1A is crucial for synaptogenesis and downstream synapse maintenance. Mutations in KIF1A cause KIF1A-associated neurological disorder (KAND). We employed isogenic gene-edited human-induced pluripotent stem cell -derived neurons to assess the effects of disparate pathogenic mutations in KIF1A on synaptic trafficking and function. Null (p.C92*) and hypoactive (p.P305L) mutations delay neurite outgrowth, mislocalize synaptic cargoes, and decrease synapse density. Conversely, a hyperactive (p.R350G) mutation supports neurite outgrowth but causes aberrant motility of synaptic vesicle precursors and deficits in microtubule-dependent presynaptic patterning. Functional analysis of neuronal activity reveals delayed synaptic maturation in loss-of-function mutations (p.P305L, p.C92*) and precocious activity in the hyperactive p.R350G mutation. These data provide insights into how KIF1A mutations with distinct molecular-level impacts lead to significant downstream synaptic deficits in human neurons.

primary.title: TMEM106B risk converges on C-terminal fragment homeostasis: genetics, mechanisms and therapy.
primary.abstract: TMEM106B is a genetic modifier influencing susceptibility to multiple neurodegenerative disorders, including frontotemporal lobar degeneration with TDP-43 pathology (FTLD-TDP), Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy, as well as contributing to healthy brain aging and neuronal reserve. The gene harbours single nucleotide polymorphisms and structural variants that define risk and protective haplotypes, and despite extensive efforts to identify the functional variant within these haplotypes, consensus remains elusive. In this review, we synthesize current knowledge of TMEM106B genetics from human cohorts and mechanistic studies, highlighting how variants may influence its regulatory network and protein levels, with an emphasis on its aggregation-prone C-terminal domain. We further integrate evidence on the roles of TMEM106B within the endo-lysosomal system and beyond, including insights into protein structure, posttranslational modifications, interactors, proteolytic processing, and fibril formation. These findings are contextualized using data from mouse and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models, highlighting current gaps in the available models and the advances required to study its functions and cleavage. Finally, we explore therapeutic strategies targeting TMEM106B, focusing on modulation of expression, specific functional pathways, and fibril formation.

primary.title: Tau-induced mitochondrial reverse electron transport drives neurodegeneration.
primary.abstract: Hyperphosphorylation and aggregation of tau are pathological hallmarks of tauopathies. Mitochondrial dysfunction is also a common feature of tauopathies. The mechanistic link between tau abnormalities and mitochondrial dysfunction and its relationship to the physiological function of tau, however, is unclear. Here, we demonstrate that tau regulates mitochondrial reverse electron transport (RET), which produces excess reactive oxygen species (ROS), reduces the NAD+/NADH ratio, and is activated by aging or stress. In flies, mice, and human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived neurons, tau depletion eliminates stress-induced RET and confers resilience. Mechanistically, tau enters mitochondria and directly interacts with the complex I subunit NDUFS3 to promote RET in a phosphorylation-dependent manner. Elevated RET further drives tau hyperphosphorylation, establishing a self-perpetuating pathological loop. Inhibition of RET ameliorates tau toxicity across species. RET regulation thus represents a previously unrecognized normal function of tau that becomes pathological in disease, providing a therapeutic target for various conditions characterized by tau abnormalities and mitochondrial dysfunction.

secondary.title: Constructing functional neural circuits to model amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with induced pluripotent stem cell-derived brain organoids.
secondary.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a progressive neurodegenerative disease characterized by the degeneration of both upper and lower motor neurons. Recent advances in human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived brain organoids offer an innovative platform to model amyotrophic lateral sclerosis in a human-specific context. These three-dimensional organoid systems allow for the study of neuronal circuit-level dysfunction, which is central to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis pathogenesis, by incorporating multiple neuronal subtypes and supporting glial populations. In particular, the integration of region-specific brain organoids into assembloid models has enabled the reconstruction of functional long-range projections and cortico-motor circuits, closely resembling human neural connectivity. This review summarizes the generation and application of human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived brain organoids for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis research, with a focus on the reconstruction of neural circuits, multi-omics profiling, and functional assays. We also discuss how organoid systems can be leveraged for drug discovery and personalized medicine in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, highlighting their potential to unveil human-specific disease mechanisms. Lastly, we address the current challenges and future directions for improving the physiological relevance of organoid models in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis research.
